articles.title: Are Redundant Labels Helpful during Category Learning? Replication of Lupyan, Rakison, & McClelland (2007)
articles.authors: Caroline Kaicher; Ellen Markman; Laura Gwilliams
articles.abstract: Labels are often advantageous for category learning. However, this may not be true for children as they learn subordinate, fine-grained object categories. In preparation for future research on subordinate category learning in children, we aimed to refine a procedure investigating the label advantage during subordinate category learning in adults. Thus, we conducted an online replication of Experiment 2 from Lupyan, Rakison, & McClelland (2007), which compares category learning under an auditory or written label condition versus a no label and non-linguistic cue condition in adults. We failed to replicate the key result, that those who received labels learned the categories faster.

articles.title: Collective Victimhood Beliefs and Policy Support Across Conflict-Affected Societies
articles.authors: Sarah Zahreddine; Sandra Penić; Rezarta Bilali
articles.abstract: Collective victimhood beliefs may have different implications for conflict-related policy support depending on how groups interpret their own and others’ suffering. Using cross-sectional survey data from 12,499 respondents across 14 ethnonational groups in 10 conflict-affected societies, we examined four single-item indicators: conflict-specific and global competitive victimhood, perceived parity in suffering, and recognition of victims’ shared human status despite differences in victimization. Pooled multilevel models and group-specific regressions assessed associations with support for reconciliation, intergroup equality, and aggression-related policies. Consistent with preregistered hypotheses, both competitive beliefs were positively associated with aggression, whereas both inclusive beliefs were positively associated with reconciliation and equality. Human-level inclusion had higher mean ratings than parity-based inclusion in 12 of 14 groups and showed stronger positive associations with reconciliation and equality and a stronger negative association with aggression. Its association with aggression was negative in all 14 groups, although association magnitudes varied. Exploratory analyses identified weaker associations between human-level inclusion and equality in active-conflict settings and more negative associations between conflict-specific competitive victimhood and equality among relatively higher-power groups, although contextual comparisons involved only 10 settings. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing recognition of shared humanity from judgments of equivalent suffering.

articles.title: TuneTwins: An Intrinsically Motivating Game Paradigm for Scalable Music Cognition Research
articles.authors: Jiaxin Li; David John Baker; John Ashley Burgoyne; Henkjan Honing
articles.abstract: Researchers across the behavioral sciences are increasingly using games as a means of data collection. Intrinsically motivating digital games are especially promising for music cognition, where large, diverse, and engaged samples are needed. In this article, we focus on a specific class of game paradigms suited to cross-cultural contexts and applicable across the developmental lifespan: auditory matching-pairs (Memory) games. We present the conception, design, and initial evaluation of TuneTwins, a solitaire auditory matching-pairs paradigm developed to study musical memory and auditory cognition. Building on self-determination theory and prior game-based research, TuneTwins employs an 8-pair (4 × 4) board to balance playability with psychometric sensitivity. Our web-based auditory adaptation introduces clear visual–auditory mappings, a three-click turn structure, and a dual scoring system that distinguishes memorized matches from lucky guesses and memory errors. Large-scale simulations of chance and optimal strategies guided the choice of board size, demonstrating that this configuration yields meaningful separation between performance extremes while avoiding ceiling effects. We further report empirical evidence from three implementations: a proof-of-concept online study, a cross-cultural field study with Mbendjele BaYaka hunter-gatherers, and an online global deployment. Across these settings, TuneTwins captured systematic performance differences between stimulus conditions and elicited high voluntary engagement, including repeated play and the completion of multiple difficulty levels. We argue that matching-pairs games such as TuneTwins provide an engaging, intuitive, and scalable paradigm for collecting behavioral data using primarily auditory stimuli—and that they can be used to probe the mental representation of music across cultures, across development, and potentially across species.

articles.title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
articles.authors: Thomas H Costello; Nathaniel Rabb; Michael Nicholas Stagnaro; Gordon Pennycook; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, U.S. adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1042) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multi-turn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found some suggestive evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in some—but not all—analyses of different conspiratorial beliefs one to two months later. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, cognitively-focused interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

articles.title: Children’s quantification of time with the comparative “more”
articles.authors: Kosta Boskovic; David Barner
articles.abstract: Events can be quantified along several dimensions— E.g., walking can be measured by number of steps taken, distance traveled, or time spent walking. In quantifying events with the comparative “more” (e.g., “Who did more walking?”), one must first identify the relevant dimension of quantification and encode each magnitude, before projecting them onto a common scale of degrees to support linguistic comparison. In the current study, we asked whether young children are able to do so for duration, which may be less salient than number or space. While previous work has established that children quantify number and space with “more” by 3 ½ years old, it is unknown whether children are able to quantify duration around this age, or whether this ability emerges later in development, perhaps closer to when children learn duration words such as “minute” and “hour” around 6 or 7 years old. In three studies, we asked children to identify who did “more” of an action (e.g., stretching) performed by two actors for varying durations. We found that children could quantify duration with “more” by 3 or 4 years old. These results suggest that children can identify time as the relevant dimension of quantification and encode a comparison of the magnitude of durations linguistically years before mastering duration words, and around when they become able to quantify magnitudes in more concrete domains such as number and space.

articles.title: Activities and their role in recovery for people with psychosis on acute mental health wards… and beyond: A mixed qualitative methods study.
articles.authors: Ciara Regan; Una Foye; Geoff Brennan; Julie Williams; Elizabeth Tuudah; Caroline Collins; Charlie Costa; LeRoy McAnuff; Lilli Underwood; Katherine Barrett
articles.abstract: Activities and their role in recovery for people with psychosis on acute mental health wards… and beyond: A mixed qualitative methods study

articles.title: The effects of non-pharmacological school-based interventions on educational outcomes in children and young people with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analysis
articles.authors: Dixiao Zhang; Dimitra Hartas; Olympia Palikara; Vasileios Sideropoulos
articles.abstract: Children and young people (CYP) with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often face inequalities when accessing learning opportunities. The evidence base is mixed on the effectiveness of school-based interventions for CYP with ADHD on academic progress gains, improved attendance, and enhanced wellbeing. We conducted a meta-analysis to specify whether school-based interventions improve the educational outcomes of CYP with ADHD. Seven databases were searched until 2nd of October 2026. The review followed the PRISMA guidelines. Of the 2164 items identified, only 16 studies were included in our analysis as they met our inclusion criteria: a) CYP with ADHD aged 5-17 years old; b) school-based interventions; c) randomized controlled trials; and d) educational outcomes. Given the substantial heterogeneity across intervention types, the findings show an inconclusive pattern of what works and what doesn’t. Our main model demonstrated that overall school-based interventions showed a small effect on educational outcomes amongst CYP with ADHD. No significant moderators, such as intervention types and outcome domains, were detected. Future research should examine the broader contextual, educational, and environmental factors associated with better educational outcomes amongst CYP with ADHD, with the aim of developing more evidence-informed and targeted interventions.

articles.title: Beyond Platforms: Assessing the Value of a Cross-Platform Perspective on SNS and Mental Health
articles.authors: Alexandra Masciantonio; Alexandra S. Wormley; Ethan; Philippe Verduyn
articles.abstract: Research on social networking sites (SNS) and mental health has produced highly heterogeneous findings, often attributed to differences between platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok. In response, cross-platform comparisons are increasingly proposed as a promising analytical direction, yet their actual conceptual and explanatory value remains unclear. Rather than aiming to identify platform-specific effects, this Short Report critically examines whether a cross-platform perspective meaningfully advances our understanding of SNS-mental health associations. To this end, we conduct a brief scoping review of quantitative studies that explicitly compare multiple SNS platforms within the same design (N = 14). The review reveals substantial methodological and conceptual inconsistencies across studies, suggesting that platform-level comparisons alone rarely clarify observed heterogeneity. We argue that future research would benefit from moving beyond platform labels toward a feature- and affordance-based cross-platform approach that is more closely aligned with psychological theory.

articles.title: Quantifying metacognition with the hmetad package in R
articles.authors: Kevin O'Neill; Stephen M Fleming
articles.abstract: A longstanding goal in metacognition research is the quantification of confidence-related parameters independently from task performance. While there is now a proliferation of generative models of confidence in numerous psychological tasks, the meta-d' model remains a popular approach to estimating metacognitive sensitivity and metacognitive bias within a signal detection theoretic framework. However, as questions in metacognition research increase in complexity, it remains an ongoing challenge to develop extensions of the meta-d' model built to deal with longitudinal, repeated-measures, or other complex experimental designs. Here we introduce the open-source R package hmetad, which allows users to fit the meta-d' model for a wide range of experimental designs using a familiar formula syntax. We also review how the meta-d'  model can be validated in a Bayesian workflow which investigates posterior estimates of key parameters. Overall, the hmetad package offers a comprehensive interface to fitting, evaluating, and visualizing signal detection theoretic models of metacognition.

articles.title: Deixis in the Graphic Domain - Young Children’s Comprehension of Arrows and Markers
articles.authors: Gregor Kachel; Cathal O'Madagain; Daniel Haun; Manuel Bohn
articles.abstract: Growing up in graphically saturated environments, children encounter arrows and markers daily. We probe their developing mastery of these symbols by continuously sampling children between two and six years of age in object-choice tasks. Study 1 (N = 72; 24–59 months) establishes that children can read both arrows and markers just before their third birthday. By pitting spatial proximity against pointing direction in ambiguous displays, Study 2 (N = 98; 25–72 months) reveals a striking shift: children favor proximity until age four, only prioritizing direction by age five. Study 3 (N = 48; 36–59 months) demonstrates that this transition coincides with the ability to generalize directional interpretations to novel symbols, suggesting that this age marks the beginning of abstract symbol interpretation. Together, these studies track the development of young children’s comprehension of deixis in the graphic domain – one of the earliest forms of graphic communication children acquire.

articles.title: PraBat: An item response theory-based test battery to assess individual differences in pragmatic abilities in preschool children from different cultural backgrounds
articles.authors: Chiara Carraro; Paula Waffen; Pelin Küçükerdoğan; Elif Ayça Yiğit; Mayurbhai Jakharabhai Odedra; Henriette Zeidler; Aylin C. Küntay; Bahar Koymen; Daniel Haun; Manuel Bohn
articles.abstract: Pragmatic abilities allow us to use and comprehend language in interaction. The assessment of individual differences in pragmatic abilities, both within and across cultural settings, is crucial to understanding how they develop. However, tools with good psychometric properties that suit this purpose are lacking. The current study describes the creation of a test battery assessing individual differences in 3- to 6-year-old children from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds. The battery is implemented as a tablet-based game, administrable both online and in person. Children are prompted by a character with one or multiple utterances and respond by selecting a picture among three options on a screen. An initial larger item pool was piloted in Germany and Kenya to ensure the items’ cross-cultural adaptability. We then used item response modeling on a sample of 713 German children to select items that varied in difficulty and fit the Rasch model. The so-constructed 19-item battery shows excellent model fit, test-retest reliability and convergent validity. The way the battery was created allows for easy cross-cultural adaptation, easy administration and scoring, thereby addressing an important gap in the developmental study of the interplay between social cognition and language. All materials and code are freely accessible to interested researchers. The task can be used via the following website: https://devpsy.web.leuphana.de/prabat/.

articles.title: Beyond Average Behaviour: Trust and Reciprocity Dynamics Reveal Distinct Behavioural Phenotypes
articles.authors: Ismail Guennouni; Tobias Nolte; Maarten Speekenbrink; Georgia Koppe; Stephen Pilling; Judy Leibowitz; P. Read Montague; Peter Fonagy
articles.abstract: Cooperation depends not only on how much people trust and reciprocate, but on how it is maintained and repaired after rupture. We analysed a 10-round Trust Game in participants with borderline personality disorder (BPD), an affective-symptom sample (AD), and community controls (N = 1,300 participants contributing 1,310 games; BPD n = 468, AD n = 556, controls n = 286 games), using mixed-effects and hidden Markov models. Average behaviour was broadly similar across groups, although AD trustees returned more than controls. As investors, BPD participants adjusted less to feedback than controls. Among trustees, AD differed most clearly from BPD: AD trustees followed cooperative response patterns more often, resumed cooperation more readily after exploitative returns, and had higher model-implied long-run cooperation at low and moderate partner investments. The occupancy and repair differences persisted when hidden states were estimated without diagnostic information, but not when BPD was restricted to interview-confirmed cases. AD–control differences in cooperative patterns did not persist among participants tested online. BPD–control differences in maintaining and restoring cooperation were smaller and depended on investment and hidden-state specification. Clinical differences were more evident in interaction dynamics than in average behaviour.

articles.title: Evaluating the mobile MUSE EEG headband for studying resting state EEG and event-related potentials
articles.authors: Ben Godde
articles.abstract:
We examined whether and how tactile EEG experiments could be done through self-assessments by participants at home or through online experiments with consumer-grade mobile EEG devices. As a first step towards this aim, we performed a Flanker task in an online scenario with a MUSE headband and similarly a conventional lab experiment with a standard EEG device.
Five undergraduate students participated in a visual flanker experiment and associated ERP components were recorded with either a standard 32-channel EEG System or a 4-channel MUSE EEG headband. In addition, we performed a 2-minutes resting state recording.
Resting state brain oscillations measured with the Muse device revealed a similar pattern as with a standard EEG machine, however, strength of alpha oscillations was significantly reduced. For the Flanker task, in the Muse data, the stimulus-locked ERP components were less visible as compared to standard EEG, still the N200 was clearly expressed for the correct trials. Interestingly, in the incorrect trials, time-locked to the response there was the same negative Ne component visible as for the standard experiment. 
Our results reveal that the Muse device is suitable to obtain event-related potentials – even from interpolated electrode channels. Advanced preprocessing and artifact removal algorithms specifically targeting such devices with only a few and peripheral channels might help to better isolate ERP components of interest. It remains the challenge to develop devices and procedures for online tactile testing.

articles.title: Racial resentment uniquely characterizes White Americans’ support for Donald Trump
articles.authors: David Michael Amodio; Jeffrey Jordan Berg; Lee Q. Cui; Andreas Schuck; Anke Stoll; Madalina Vlasceanu
articles.abstract: Despite the popular narrative that White Americans supported Donald Trump in 2016 due to economic concerns, several studies show that their support is more strongly predicted by a variety of social issues concerning race and gender. The present work sought to characterize the core features of these social issues among White Americans by assessing 15 self-report and behavioral measures of social attitudes, in addition to several economic, political, and demographic indicators, and comparing their relative effects on Trump support during the Biden and second Trump presidential terms. In both studies, conducted in 2022 (N=906) and 2026 (N=1206), racial resentment was the strongest predictor of Trump support relative to all other measures of social, economic, and political concerns. Economic stress was negatively associated with Trump support. Furthermore, we find that, among conservatives, the relation between racial resentment and Trump support aligns more closely with MAGA identity than with conservatism generally. These findings clarify the nature of White Americans’ support for Trump, show its sustained association across presidential administrations, and link it closely to the MAGA movement.

articles.title: The Timing and Frequency of Instruction to Foster New Learning: Comparing Cognitive and Motivational Strategies in Category Learning
articles.authors: Kyosuke Kakinuma; Keise Izuma
articles.abstract: Effective instruction should not only enhance immediate performance but also prepare learners to succeed when learning independently in novel situations (new learning). This study examined which timing and frequency strategies of instruction most effectively foster new learning. We compared six strategies, inspired by theories of motivation (e.g., self-determination theory) and cognition (e.g., testing effect), with two control conditions (no-instruction and full-instruction). Across three experiments (total N = 1,522), participants performed a category learning task. They first received instruction through feature highlighting, whose timing and frequency varied across conditions. Subsequently, their performance was assessed in an independent session where they learned new categories without instruction. An adaptive strategy that tailored instruction to learner performance significantly outperformed the control conditions in initial experiments (Experiments 1 and 2). However, this effect was not observed in a comprehensive experiment (Experiment 3), suggesting that adaptivity itself may not have been the beneficial factor. Instead, an overall examination suggested that the beneficial effects were attributable to two underlying instructional patterns shared by the conditions that outperformed the control conditions: (1) providing instruction in successive sequences, and (2) interspersing tests without instruction by restricting the frequency of instruction. Instructional strategies with these two patterns yielded a significant advantage over the control conditions for independently discovering correct knowledge in novel situations, although they did not reliably improve generalization of that knowledge to other items. This integration of instructional patterns appears to foster new learning by balancing the useful information from instruction with the desirable difficulty of testing.

articles.title: Demarcation: conspiracy theories and misinformation
articles.authors: Alessandro Miani; Stephan Lewandowsky
articles.abstract: Misinformation and conspiracy theories are often treated as interchangeable, but they have different predictors and respond differently to correction. We identify their differences at the level of the claim itself rather than at what these claims trigger in the mind of the believer. Whereas misinformation claims are, in principle, assessable against a ground truth, conspiracy theories are claims wrapped in an explanation for why evidence is absent or untrustworthy. This semantic criterion avoids conflating bare falsehoods with conspiracy theories while preserving the distinctive structural features of the latter. We show how the wrapper grants conspiracy theories a degree of immunity from disconfirmation and why a claim-level demarcation can inform both theory and measurement.

articles.title: The Future of Social (Dis)Connection
articles.authors: Micaela Rodriguez; Scott W. Campbell; Amie Michelle Gordon
articles.abstract: Over the next decades, the nature of and possibilities for social connection will rapidly evolve with advances in artificial intelligence, mixed-reality technologies, and pervasive digital integration. Accordingly, psychological science must update how it conceptualizes and measures social connection. Here, we advance a three-part conceptual framework for understanding social (dis)connection in contemporary and future environments. First, we situate social experiences within a dynamic relational ecosystem—a system of interaction partners and channels, ambient social cues, and sociocultural contexts that together shape connection. Second, we conceptualize “alone” and “together” not as binary states but as a gradient shaped by level of physical copresence and communication (shades of aloneness and togetherness). Third, we conceptualize discrete social interactions as multidimensional, characterized by features such as interaction partner, relationship type, medium, temporality, engagement, and volition. Building on this framework, we propose five testable predictions about how social (dis)connection may evolve in the coming decades: the decoupling of objective and subjective connection, the erosion of “pure” solitude, the increasing effortfulness and value of in-person interaction, the fragmentation of shared reality, and the growing taken-for-grantedness of connection. We conclude by discussing methodological and applied implications of this framework.

articles.title: The analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis: a framework, open tools, and a screening study
articles.authors: Zack van Allen
articles.abstract:
Background. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to apply predefined codebooks to qualitative data, and studies of this practice usually report agreement with human coding for a single configuration. However, each configuration rests on many defensible choices (e.g., how the task is worded, how the codebook is presented, and how agreement is scored), and the extent to which results depend on these choices remains relatively unknown.

Methods. I describe the analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis (i.e., the set of defensible configurations for producing and scoring codes), define what a multiverse study should report, propose a staged design for exploring it, and release two open-source tools, QualFrame and QualBench, that record each choice as a setting and score every run. In a screening study, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna coded 40 open-access smoking-cessation trial reports for 94 behaviour change techniques under a half-fraction factorial design that varied task instructions, codebook division, reasoning effort, instruction wording, and code order, with repeat runs of one configuration. Agreement with historical Human Behaviour-Change Project annotations was measured with the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). Exploratory analyses examined majority votes and earlier runs of four models on 50 reports excluded from screening.

Results. Across 32 configurations (38 runs; recorded API spend US$13.66), MCC ranged from 0.24 to 0.57. Four runs of one configuration varied by at most 0.02 in MCC; however, of the codes applied by at least one of these runs, 43% to 64% were not applied by all four. Within this design, the contrasts for task instructions, reasoning effort, and codebook division each exceeded the average difference between the two models, and their effects depended on one another and on the model; for example, asking the model to decide on every code raised MCC by 0.10 with the whole codebook but by 0.02 with the codebook divided. The apparent cost of dividing the codebook fell from 0.045 to 0.011 when scoring was restricted to the 12 techniques the annotators prioritized, and balanced accuracy ranked a different configuration best. Earlier runs of four models with similar agreement on the screening reports diverged on the 50 excluded reports, where their majority vote had agreement similar to the best model.

Conclusions. Agreement with a reference depended on configuration choices, their interactions, the scoring scope, and the reports scored. Studies of AI-assisted coding should report the configurations they explored and test whether their conclusions survive these choices. To build a cumulative evidence base, I propose a research agenda that others can take up independently with the open tools and a common reporting format.

articles.title: Ten Years Later: Multiple Stigmas and Rental Discrimination in Germany. A Replication and Extension of Mazziotta, Zerr, and Rohmann (2015)
articles.authors: Kristin Jankowsky; Ola Amin; Emilija Mladenovic; Maik Ottmers; Agostino Mazziotta
articles.abstract: In an online field experiment (N = 589 rental listings), we replicated Study 2 of Mazziotta, Zerr, and Rohmann (2015) on ethnicity, sexual orientation, and their intersection as sources of rental discrimination in Germany. Extending the design, listings were sampled from cities with low versus high vote shares for the radical-right AfD. Ten years after the original, a Turkish heterosexual couple again received fewer replies (59% vs. 73%) and fewer invitations to viewings (39% vs. 58%) than a German heterosexual couple (ω = .15 and .19). As in the original, we found no significant discrimination based on sexual orientation and no evidence that holding both minority statuses reduced discrimination. Ethnic discrimination did not differ significantly between low- and high-AfD-share cities.

articles.title: Reduced Visual Imagery Vividness as a Risk Factor for PTSD: Implications for Aphantasia and Imagery-Based Treatments
articles.authors: Diane Swick; Sandy Lwi; Jary Larsen
articles.abstract: Recent theoretical models such as the generative adversarial framework propose that the ability to generate high-fidelity visual images may intensify the severity of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), particularly the intrusive re-experiencing of traumatic events. Meanwhile, individuals with minimal imagery (aphantasia) may be protected. To evaluate this relationship, 312 Veterans completed the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire (VVIQ) and the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5). Results indicated that lower VVIQ scores (less vivid imagery) were associated with greater PTSD severity. This inverse relationship was observed across all PTSD symptom clusters, with the strongest association for the negative cognition/mood cluster. Five of the eight Veterans who reported very low VVIQ scores (consistent with aphantasia) had clinically significant PTSD and high levels of intrusive symptoms, further indicating that aphantasia was not protective. These findings have implications for PTSD treatments and suggest that reduced visual imagery is associated with impaired processing of traumatic experiences.

articles.title: Open Science in Canada:  Mapping Knowledge, Attitudes, Perceptions, and Implementation
articles.authors: Nicolás Alessandroni; Krista Byers-Heinlein
articles.abstract: Open science is a national priority in Canada, yet the transition from policy to practice depends on understanding the researchers whose behaviour these policies seek to change. We report a nationwide survey that comprehensively assesses the state of open science across Canadian higher education. Researchers and trainees recruited through 18 institutions (N = 705) rated 13 open science practices across five dimensions: awareness, knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and implementation. Roughly one in three respondents had never heard of open science before the survey. Among those who had, attitudes were consistently positive and there was a widespread desire to learn more, but self-assessed knowledge was low and concentrated in two long-established practices — open access and open-source software — and implementation exceeded 20% for only four of the 13 practices. Researchers pointed to a lack of training and know-how, rather than a lack of interest, as the primary barriers. Two further patterns compounded these gaps: respondents underestimated how favourably their peers viewed open science while overestimating how much their peers practised it, and their stated intentions for the coming year ran well ahead of historically observed rates of adoption. Together, these findings describe a research community that is willing but underequipped and largely unaware of its own consensus, indicating that the main barriers to open science in Canada lie in capacity and perception rather than attitudes.

articles.title: Differential effects of individual versus consensus evaluations of narrator-to-story fit on the experience and outcomes of narrative listening.
articles.authors: Carolyn McGettigan; Khadija Faiz; Amy Francis; Elizabeth Leivers; Laurie Sin; Hannah Jones; Nadine Lavan; Saloni Krishnan
articles.abstract: While a reader might imagine the narrator's and characters' voices in a written book, a spoken narrative solidifies the relationship between the narrator and the text. Here, we report two experiments investigating how perceived narrator-to-story fit affects narrative listening enjoyment and other listening outcomes. In a first experiment (N=400 participants), we manipulated the gender-related congruence between the expected and heard narrator of four spoken narratives in a willingness-to-wait paradigm. We found that listeners were more likely to continue listening to congruent than incongruent stories, but did not enjoy them more or comprehend them more accurately. However, we observed a dissociation in the observed effects of perceived narrator-to-story fit: specifically, higher individual evaluations significantly increased enjoyment, while both higher individual and (aggregated) mean fit ratings predicted greater motivation to continue listening. This suggested that crowd-sourced data may be less effective than personal taste when predicting narrative listening enjoyment. Indeed, a second experiment using a larger number of stories showed that participants’ enjoyment of spoken narratives is most strongly predicted by within-sample individual fit ratings, but not by within- or between-group aggregate ratings. Our findings provide evidence to support personalisation of narration as a way to promote enjoyment of spoken narratives and, potentially, audiobooks.

articles.title: Social media use is associated with lower positive and higher negative affect in young people: The roles of active and passive use and anhedonia
articles.authors: Xueqing Ma; Angad Sahni; Ciara McCabe
articles.abstract: Evidence on the associations between social media use (SMU) and youth affect remains inconsistent, partly because it remains unclear how active versus passive engagement differs in daily life, whether these relationships are bidirectional, and how individual characteristics such as gender and mental health symptoms moderate them. We utilized ecological momentary assessment (EMA) via a smartphone app to sample real-world affect and SMU (active [posting/messaging] vs. passive [browsing]) among 80 young people (Mean age=20.1 years) with varying depression and anhedonia, yielding 2,316 observations across six consecutive days. Multilevel regressions revealed that, concurrently, SMU was associated with lower positive affect (PA; β=-0.35, p<.001) and higher negative affect (NA; β=0.22, p=.002). Crucially, this negative affect association was weaker among individuals with higher depression (β=-0.02, p=.04) but stronger among those with higher anhedonia (β=0.04, p=.02). Conversely, active (vs. passive) use was concurrently linked to higher PA (β=4.12, p<.001) and lower NA (β=-2.01, p=.05), with these favourable associations stronger among males than females and among individuals with lower depression symptoms (β=0.06, p=.03). In time-lagged analyses, higher PA predicted a lower subsequent likelihood of active versus passive use (β=-1.23, p=.01), while SMU itself did not predict subsequent affect. These findings emphasize that while general SMU coincides with less favourable affect, active engagement might offer situational benefits over passive browsing. Crucially, these dynamic relationships depend heavily on gender and distinct psychological vulnerabilities, demonstrating the necessity of distinguishing depression from anhedonia in digital mental health research.

articles.title: Exposure to Sexualised Appearance and Beauty Content on Social Media and Body Satisfaction in Female Adolescents: A Computational Real-World Approach
articles.authors: Christina Haag; Mingyue Zha; Matti Vuorre; Laura Boeschoten; Amanda M Ferguson; Sebastian Kurten; Amelia Leyland-Craggs; Valerie Yap; Jasmine Fardouly; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Experimental studies show that viewing idealised bodies on social media can lower body satisfaction, but whether this extends to the content adolescents actually encounter is unknown, because studies of everyday exposure have relied on self-report rather than on what was actually viewed. In an observational study, we combined TikTok data donation with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment in 66 female adolescents aged 14–18. A locally run computer vision pipeline classified the visual content of 242,422 watched videos for thin and sexualised female bodies – coding the imagery itself rather than hashtags or captions – and metadata-based classifiers identified beauty-filter use and TikTok’s own beauty-related content labels. Content meeting the body criterion made up under one minute of roughly 91 watched minutes per day. Across all three measures, daily exposure was not associated with end-of-day body satisfaction, within or between persons, nor was morning body satisfaction associated with subsequent exposure. Everyday exposure to appearance ideals may be too sparse and too stable from day to day for day-level designs to detect any effect of it.

articles.title: When the brain can change: effects of neuroplasticity education on beliefs about brain-based mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery. We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs. Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control. The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2. The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall. The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders. In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance. These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.

articles.title: Selective Exposure to Environmental Messages: Dual Sentiment Pathways to Information-Seeking Intentions
articles.authors: Changyu Jing; Suzanne Oosterwijk; Disa Sauter
articles.abstract: Environmental problems are intensifying, prompting expanded public communication efforts to raise awareness and motivate pro-environmental behavior. However, meaningful engagement with environmental messages is often selective, as people actively choose among many competing messages. In this paper, we examined how active engagement with environmental messages related to affective orientations (i.e., sentiments) towards environmental issues. Through a selective exposure paradigm, participants selected from four types of environmental messages varying in valence (positive vs. negative) and personal relevance (human vs. animal). We expected that engagement with these messages would be associated with changes in hopeful and anxious sentiments toward environmental issues. These sentiment shifts, in turn, were expected to predict the likelihood of participants seeking further environmental information. In an initial exploratory study (N = 283), participants’ selection of the different kinds of environmental messages showed no direct effect on environmental information-seeking intentions. Further analyses revealed two competing indirect paths: (a) increased seeking intentions via enhanced anxious sentiments and (b) reduced seeking intentions via diminished hopeful sentiments. These patterns were replicated in a confirmatory study (N = 1,009), demonstrating their robustness. Together, these findings suggest that the effectiveness of environmental communication is not limited to valence-congruent sentiments. Instead, the balance of emotional reactions that messages trigger shapes information-seeking behavior.

articles.title: Resting-state alpha scale-free dynamics predict individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values during free choice
articles.authors: Jianhong Zhu; Junya Hashimoto; Tatsuru Honda; Kazuki Yamamoto; Mayo Anno; Georg Northoff; Takashi Nakao
articles.abstract: Values learned through reward can continue to influence choices guided by one's own preferences, such as which painting to hang, to an extent that varies across individuals. Because such preferences build up gradually across choices, their expression may depend on how well internally generated states are sustained over time, a property indexed by long-range temporal correlations (LRTC) in intrinsic brain activity. We tested whether resting-state alpha-band LRTC predicts individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values. Eighty-one participants learned through probabilistic feedback which of four abstract shapes tended to be rewarded, and then judged their preferences among these shapes and 11 new shapes without feedback. Alpha LRTC was estimated by detrended fluctuation analysis of resting-state electroencephalography recorded before, between, and after the tasks. A trial-level mixed-effects model showed that reward history influenced preference judgments and that this influence decreased with resting-state alpha LRTC: participants with weak LRTC chose high-reward shapes over new shapes on 75% of trials, whereas those with strong LRTC were close to indifference (54%). The relationship was distributed across the scalp, stable across recordings, and not explained by spectral power or learning performance. Resting-state alpha LRTC is thus related to how strongly reward-learned values are carried into preference-based choice. Given the view that stronger LRTC reflects a longer window over which internally generated states are integrated, the observed relationship could arise because the window is biased toward values built up through one's own choices, or because it attenuates values learned under a criterion that no longer applies; which account holds remains to be determined.

articles.title: Development and validation of a task for assessing help-seeker relational dynamics.
articles.authors: Tyler Kwan; Jae Shin; Caroline Selai; Orestis Zavlis; Michael Moutoussis
articles.abstract: Self-other evaluations play a crucial role in understanding psychiatric disorders and improving collaboration between service users and providers. However, experimental paradigms of such relational processes tend to have low reliability and ecological validity. Quantitative analyses can validate the task’s measurement properties while qualitative analyses can empower service users to provide novel insights about task development and interpretation. In this study, we use both quantitative and qualitative analyses to develop the “Helping Task” based on the iterated prisoner’s dilemma. In this task, help-seeking participants knowingly engaged in an asymmetric relationship with a computerized help-provider, in which both parties invested effort (points). Initial qualitative feedback from 17 individuals (15 ‘neurotypical’, 2 having lived experience of relational difficulties) was used to refine key task properties (like task instructions, interface labels, and general navigation). Subsequent thematic analyses revealed that these participants interpreted helping exchanges through expectations about reciprocity, moral obligations, and underlying mental intentions, mirroring descriptions of real helping relationships. Moreover, quantitative analyses of 30 online participants validated the task’s sensitivity to helper behaviour and the within-session reliability of mean trust, decision satisfaction, and intended effort. Finally, computational analyses revealed probabilistic states in which trust, decision satisfaction, and effort were jointly lower or higher, indicating that self-other evaluations were linked to willingness to invest in the relationship. These findings support the reliability and validity of the Helping Task and pave the way for computational studies of self-other evaluations in helping relationships.

articles.title: No evidence that positive outcomes elicit a stronger sense of agency once correcting for publication bias: a commentary on, and re-analysis of, Mariano et al. (2025)
articles.authors: Robrecht van der Wel; Shaheed Azaad; Pernille Hemmer; John Michael
articles.abstract: In a recent meta-analysis, Mariano et al. (2025) conclude that people experience a stronger sense of agency over positive than negative outcomes, indexed by temporal compression. In this commentary, we evaluate that claim and identify several concerns about its validity. First, we argue that temporal compression effects should be standardized before being combined, because values in milliseconds are not necessarily comparable across different paradigms. When we analyzed standardized effects, evidence for a valence effect was absent once adjusting for publication bias. Second, we identified data integrity issues, identifying several studies that were included but either (1) did not manipulate outcome valence at all, or (2) contained only a positive or negative condition compared to a neutral condition. Excluding these studies meant that even unstandardized effects did not support Mariano et al.’s headline finding.

articles.title: A set of dynamical rules for conversational progression act as a precursor to collective cognition
articles.authors: Zachary P Rosen
articles.abstract: Conversation unfolds between speakers as a series of coordinated updates from prior ideas expressed in earlier utterances to new sets of ideas. This process of speakers and conversation partners jointly updating prior "conversation states" is an important piece of the cognitive scaffolding that enables social coordination, and even collective cognition -- the capacity for individuals to pool their cognitive resources to solve problems together. However, a functional data-driven description of how this process works is missing in the extant literature. This report provides a functional description of how conversation states are updated in terms of information-theoretic processes, while analyzing a corpus of 5,447 conversations in nine typologically diverse languages. Our results show that individuals form a strongly connected distributed computational system during conversation, which generates new information according to a power-law distribution. This enables speakers to encode and solve a potentially unbounded number of problems and ideas, simply by conversing.

articles.title: Do young children represent multiple mutually exclusive possibilities?
articles.authors: Urvi Maheshwari; Caren Walker; David Barner
articles.abstract: A prominent hypothesis in the literature on logical reasoning suggests that, unlike human adults and older children, 3-year-olds deploy a “minimal representation of possibility” when reasoning about the existence of a reward in one of two possible locations. On this view, children are unable to represent two mutually exclusive possibilities simultaneously, and instead commit to one location for the reward in a pair of possible locations, only considering the second location once they have evidence that their first choice is not correct. Although this hypothesis may explain children’s struggles on various tests of modal reasoning, the idea that children may represent possible reward locations sequentially (rather than simultaneously) has not been directly tested. In two studies, we asked 24- to 38-month-olds to choose two of three reward locations, one of which was physically impossible. We found that children aged 31 to 38 months selected the two possible locations without feedback when required to make a simultaneous choice. We argue that these data are compatible with an ability to represent multiple mutually exclusive possibilities.

articles.title: Desinformación y mitos relacionados con la vacunación contra el VPH en Colombia: una revisión rápida de la literatura
articles.authors: Carla Montoya; Christopher Milbert-Beltz; Valentina Grajales; Valery Esteban; Francisco Palencia-Sánchez
articles.abstract:
Introducción: La vacunación contra el virus del papiloma humano (VPH) es fundamental para prevenir el cáncer de cuello uterino y otros cánceres asociados. En Colombia, su aceptación se ha visto afectada por mitos, desinformación y pérdida de confianza, especialmente tras el evento de El Carmen de Bolívar (2014).
Metodología: Se realizó una revisión rápida de la literatura siguiendo la guía metodológica de Cochrane y las recomendaciones PRISMA 2020. Se buscaron estudios en PubMed, SciELO, Web of Science, Embase y Scopus, además de literatura gris; la última búsqueda se realizó en agosto de 2026. Se incluyeron estudios realizados en Colombia y publicados desde 2012 que abordaran mitos y/o desinformación relacionados con la vacunación contra el VPH.
Resultados: Se incluyeron 19 estudios, organizados en tres categorías: mitos, desinformación y consecuencias sobre las tasas de vacunación. Se identificaron preocupaciones sobre la seguridad y eficacia de la vacuna, brechas de conocimiento y creencias relacionadas con la sexualidad, junto con un descenso sostenido de la cobertura desde 2014.
Discusión: La vacilación y negativa a la vacunación son multifactoriales e involucran factores cognitivos, socioculturales e institucionales. La crisis de El Carmen de Bolívar contribuyó a la pérdida de confianza, en un contexto de deficiencias previas en información, comunicación y capacitación. Sin embargo, no se ha establecido causalidad directa entre desinformación y decisiones de vacunación.
Conclusiones: La percepción de riesgo, las brechas de conocimiento y la desinformación continúan siendo barreras relevantes. La cobertura permanece por debajo de la meta de la OMS de 90 % para 2030, y estrategias como el modelo COM-B podrían contribuir a mejorar la aceptación.

articles.title: Examining the Role of Working Memory in Reasoning and Meta-reasoning:  A Fuzzy-trace approach
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Meta-reasoning, the ability to monitor progress and regulate effort during reasoning, comprises monitoring and control. Monitoring, including confidence, is assumed to guide control processes. Yet, whether monitoring and control compete with reasoning for shared cognitive resources is unclear. To address this, we examined the role of working memory in reasoning and meta-reasoning, drawing on Fuzzy Trace Theory and the meta-reasoning framework. Participants (N = 998) solved syllogisms with and without validity-believability conflict in a two-response paradigm under six constraint conditions. Accuracy declined only when load and deadline were combined. Confidence was lower on conflict than on non-conflict problems and reliably predicted answer changes and rethinking time across all conditions. Monitoring resolution, however, was low throughout. These results suggest cognitive constraints impair reasoning generally but largely spare conflict-detection and control sensitivity. Reasoners’ limited ability to discriminate correct from incorrect responses appears to reflect a general monitoring limitations rather than constrained resources.

articles_hidden.title: Proactive Academic Stress Screening in Education: NPRO-8 Core Mental Fitness Screening
articles_hidden.authors: Jerome I. Rotgans
articles_hidden.abstract: Academic stress is a longstanding concern in education, with evidence linking it to examination difficulties, disrupted sleep, and poorer wellbeing. A student support pathway that depends on students requesting help or showing visible deterioration risks intervening only after difficulties have affected daily functioning. This paper proposes NPRO-8 Core as a new approach to proactive, objective assessment of stress-related functioning in students. Its preventive rationale is to create opportunities for recognition and support before difficulties escalate. A two-tier pathway combines brief screening offered across an institution with targeted functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) assessment during structured cognitive tasks. The assessment considers Stress Load, Recovery Capacity, and Functional Impact, with repeated measurements intended to support review over time. Questionnaires provide access to students’ experiences; physiological and behavioural measures add a complementary perspective that does not depend solely on recognizing and reporting distress. The proposed contribution is to integrate these sources into a proactive student support pathway. Drawing on the preventive logic of physical-health screening, the framework links measurement to timely review and appropriate action.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Bottlenecks Improve AI Alignment with Human Moral Judgment
articles_hidden.authors: Danica Dillion; Debanjan Mondal; Wenlong Zhao; Niket Tandon; Kurt Gray
articles_hidden.abstract: As AI becomes increasingly integrated into daily life and high-stakes decision-making, aligning it with human moral judgments is a challenge of profound importance. People often mistrust AI’s moral decisions, partly because its opaque processes differ from human reasoning. We introduce “cognitive bottlenecks” that guide large language models (LLMs) to base moral judgments on a small set of psychologically meaningful features, such as perceived harm, agent intention, and victim vulnerability. Across multiple LLMs and moral frameworks, bottlenecks improved alignment with human moral judgments. Participants viewed bottleneck systems as more moral and trustworthy than systems without bottlenecks, and preferred bottleneck-generated explanations over those produced through standard chain-of-thought prompting. Bottlenecks can be implemented through prompting alone, without model retraining. These findings demonstrate the benefits of integrating psychological theory into AI and offer a scalable approach to improving AI-human alignment.

articles_hidden.title: Using Behavioral Nudges to Engage Caregivers in Digital Shared Reading and Parenting Practices: Impacts on Caregivers and Early Childhood Development
articles_hidden.authors: kaija taylor; Mary-Claire Ball; Alexia Serratore; Wardah Nadeem; Katherine Tredinnick; Natalia Kucirkova; Kaja Kinga Jasińska
articles_hidden.abstract: This study is a mixed-methods impact evaluation of a digital parenting and shared book reading intervention (Worldreader’s BookSmart app with embedded parenting tips, Vroom TipsTM) on caregivers’ self-efficacy, beliefs, and practices, and early childhood outcomes in South Africa. We further investigated whether behavioral nudges could promote sustained engagement. Study 1 consisted of a 4-arm randomized controlled trial (BookSmart, BookSmart with reminder nudges, BookSmart with goal-setting nudges, control group) where caregivers (N = 519) of children aged 3-5 years used BookSmart for 15 weeks. We found randomization to access the intervention (i.e., intent-to-treat) had no significant effect on caregiver or child outcomes. However, behavioral nudges, particularly goal-setting messages, increased caregiver engagement and improved cognitive and language skills specifically for disadvantaged children (i.e., children from lower-SES households and children with lower baseline skills). Greater intervention engagement (i.e., treatment-on-the-treated) was significantly associated with language skills and marginally associated with literacy skills. Study 2 consisted of qualitative interviews with caregivers (N = 20) before and after using BookSmart for 3 weeks. Results indicated that several barriers impacted caregivers’ engagement with the intervention, including costs (e.g., airtime) and language accessibility (e.g., caregivers reported translating English books into their native language). Our results highlight that digital reading interventions have the potential to support early childhood development, while stressing that engagement with the intervention is critical in realizing potential positive outcomes. The findings suggest that access and usage barriers should be considered when designing interventions and that behavioral nudges may serve to increase engagement.

articles_hidden.title: The Importance of Nature Across Domains of Life in Sub-Saharan Africa
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Ira Billet; Natalie Elaine Johnson; Luzelle Naude; Amber Gayle Thalmayer
articles_hidden.abstract: Human well-being depends on the natural environment, yet evidence on how nature supports human life comes almost entirely from Western, industrialized societies—not from the regions facing the greatest ecological impacts of climatic change. We assessed the importance of nature for ten life domains spanning four dimensions (Cultural, Community, Instrumental, Personal) among a sample of emerging adults in Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa (N = 2,792). Most participants rated nature as important for at least one domain, while about one-third rated nature as important for all ten. Greater importance of nature in the Cultural dimension was associated with greater life satisfaction, while greater importance in Cultural, Community, and Instrumental dimensions was associated with greater climate anxiety, over and above subjective connectedness to nature, religiosity, and socioeconomic status. Findings suggest nature plays an important role in the lives of emerging adults in Sub-Saharan Africa, which may support well-being while making the risks associated with climate change more distressing.

articles_hidden.title: Novelty Processing in Aging: Absence of an Association with Episodic Memory Abilities
articles_hidden.authors: Anaïs Servais; Christine Bastin
articles_hidden.abstract: Conceptually, novelty processing and episodic memory are closely linked. Yet it remains unclear whether they rely on common or partly independent mechanisms. We investigated whether their relationship depends on the type of novelty and representational content in healthy older adults. Seventy-eight adults aged 61–84 years completed eye-tracking tasks assessing Absolute novelty (unknown stimuli) and Associative novelty (novel configurations of familiar elements) for objects and scenes, as well as a pupillometry task assessing responses to novel objects. Novelty-processing indices were correlated with performance across various episodic memory tasks using preregistered Bayesian correlations. Older adults showed reliable gaze preferences for both Absolute and Associative novelty in object and scene tasks. Contrary to our predictions, however, Absolute novelty preference was generally unrelated to performance on familiarity-based recognition and perceptual discrimination measures hypothesized to rely on the perirhinal cortex. Associative novelty preference was likewise largely unrelated to episodic memory performance, although a small number of unexpected associations with verbal recall emerged for object novelty. Novelty-related pupil responses also showed little evidence of associations with memory performance. Exploratory comparisons with data from younger adults aged 18-30 years (from Servais & Bastin, 2026) indicated largely comparable gaze-based novelty preferences across age groups, although novelty-related peak pupil dilation was reduced in older adults. Overall, these findings suggest that individual differences in novelty processing, when assessed in paradigms with no memory confound, are largely independent of episodic memory performance in healthy older adults and that gaze-based novelty processing may remain preserved with age for both novelty types.

articles_hidden.title: “We love our jobs!” Systems Thinking and Participatory Action Research for the future of neurodiversity and skilled employment
articles_hidden.authors: Dora M Raymaker; Shawna Spain; Nybelle Caruso; Joelle Maslak; Nicole Leblanc; Morénike Giwa Onaiwu; Jonathan Spector; Passion Ilea; Julia Crown; Kristin Akervall
articles_hidden.abstract: Although neurodivergent people can achieve high levels of academic and vocational training in the same professions as others, they remain un- and under-employed; this is in part due to the “wickedness” of the problem. To address the complexity we convened a group of neurodivergent lived experience and employment experts to  1) define which problems in neurodiversity and skilled employment are most urgent to address; 2) create actionable strategies with potential leverage for generating the desired employment outcomes. We used qualitative methods from the systems thinking field: Soft Systems Methodology, futures visioning and SWOT analysis, and Group Model Building (system dynamics). The workshops resulted in identifying intervention leverage between organizational psychology constructs of employee wellbeing, workplace climate, and mutually beneficial workplace relationships, in conjunction with a new disability stress construct, rather than specific skills building or remediation of disability characteristics. Reaching a future in which neurodivergent people love their jobs will take education, resources, champions from the outside and inside, universal access, paradigm shifts, infrastructure, and recognition of individual and social complexity. We recommend examining the organizational psychology literature for adaptable interventions; focusing on peer support; leveraging emerging technology to manage complexity; and supporting supervisor behavior change based on authentic understanding.

articles_hidden.title: Inter-Sect Solidarity in Wartime Lebanon
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Zahreddine
articles_hidden.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined which interpretations of shared adversity were associated with solidarity across sectarian boundaries during the 2026 hostilities in Lebanon. In a face-to-face survey of 450 Lebanese adults (August 2026), we assessed common and intergroup threat, three formulations of inclusive victimhood, inter-sect contact, sectarianism, political interpretations, and hosting displaced people. In preregistered adjusted models, common threat was positively associated with inter-sect solidarity, whereas inter-sect and displacement-related threat were negatively associated. Common-humanity victimhood, which recognizes shared humanity despite differences in suffering, showed a substantial positive association with solidarity; beliefs that sects suffered equally showed no association. Global victimhood similarity was positively associated only when examined separately from common-humanity victimhood. Contact frequency and quality were positively associated with solidarity, whereas sectarianism was negatively associated; the hypothesized common-threat × sectarianism interaction was not supported. Lebanon–Israel framing and having hosted displaced people were also positively associated with solidarity in their respective models. In exploratory omnibus models, common-humanity victimhood, contact, and displacement-related threat retained independent associations, but common threat, sectarianism, and war framing did not. These correlational results distinguish recognizing shared vulnerability from perceiving other groups as threats and suggest that solidarity can coexist with recognition of different experiences of suffering.

articles_hidden.title: The Temporal Trajectory of Visual Perspective in Autobiographical Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Nilay Ozdemir Haksever; Peggy L. St. Jacques
articles_hidden.abstract: Autobiographical memories differ systematically with remoteness, yet little is known about the temporal form of these differences or when they are most pronounced. One consistent change over time concerns visual perspective—as memories become more remote, own-eyes perspectives become less prominent and observer-like perspectives more prominent. Because visual perspective specifies the vantage point from which a remembered event is mentally seen, these shifts may reflect changes in how visual imagery of past events is reconstructed over time. We examined the temporal trajectory of visual perspective across 18,229 autobiographical memories from 80 participants, using memory age measured in days to characterize its relationship with own-eyes and observer-like perspectives at a finer temporal resolution than in previous work. For both perspectives, age-related differences followed a negatively accelerated trajectory. Observer perspective increased and own-eyes perspective decreased most sharply among relatively recent memories, with progressively smaller differences at greater memory ages. Approximately half of the total modeled difference occurred within the first four months, although the trajectory continued across several years. Higher reliving and emotional intensity were associated with attenuated age-related shifts in both perspectives, and rehearsal also moderated their trajectories. These findings show that visual perspective varies nonlinearly across autobiographical memory age and identify the early months after an event as a particularly dynamic period. More broadly, the results characterize the temporal organization of autobiographical imagery, linking the viewpoint from which past events are visualized to both their remoteness and the subjective qualities of recollection.

articles_hidden.title: The Reciprocal Effects of Trauma-Focused Rumination and Emotional Clarity in Daily Life: A Mechanistic Evaluation Using Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Cameron Pugach; Emily Heinlein; Vera Vine; Blair Elizabeth Wisco
articles_hidden.abstract: Rumination, or the tendency to passively and repetitively think about one’s distress, is a maladaptive form of emotion regulation that confers risk for psychological disorders including posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Current theories suggest that low emotional clarity may prompt rumination. Yet, the effects of rumination on emotional clarity are less clear, with some research indicating that rumination might foster short-term benefits by increasing emotional clarity, and other research suggesting that rumination may further hamper emotional clarity. The goal of this preregistered study was to test these theoretical, within-subject pathways by applying dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) to assess the reciprocal relationships between trauma-focused rumination and emotional clarity in daily life. Experience sampling data was collected from 238 trauma-exposed college students five times per day for 14 days (NSurveys = 7918). Bivariate DSEM revealed significant reciprocal effects between trauma-focused rumination and low emotional clarity with equivalent strength of these effects. Both trauma-focused rumination and low emotional clarity demonstrated significant autoregressive effects suggesting persistence of each process over time. PTSD symptom severity was associated with higher mean levels of each process and with higher inertia of trauma-focused rumination. Beyond these main findings, several other between-subject correlations emerged that provide preliminary insights into the dynamic relationships between trauma-focused rumination and emotional clarity. Findings suggest that trauma-focused rumination and low emotional clarity are reciprocally reinforced in the short-term to keep trauma survivors stuck in their distress. The broader theoretical implications for understanding the dynamic, functional interrelationship between understanding and regulating emotions are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: MUSIMAGINE: A Standardised, Multidimensional Database for Music-Evoked Mental Imagery Research
articles_hidden.authors: Sneha Jain; Patti Nijhuis; Joshua Silberstein Bamford
articles_hidden.abstract: Music listening often evokes mental imagery involving imagined scenes, people, movement, emotions, and narratives. However, systematic research on music-evoked mental imagery (MEMI) requires resources that capture not only whether imagery occurs, but also its phenomenological characteristics, content and potential determinants. We introduce MUSIMAGINE, an open-access database designed to support multidimensional investigation of MEMI. The database comprises sixty royalty-free, 60-second instrumental excerpts selected to represent four valence-arousal quadrants, alongside data from 153 participants who listened to a subset of the excerpts. Measures include imagery occurrence; six phenomenological ratings (ease, vividness, clarity, narrativity, movement and emotion intensity); structured reports of imagery elements, sensory modalities, and emotions; open-ended descriptions; subjective music appraisal (valence, arousal, liking, familiarity); individual differences in sensory imagery ability and musical background; and acoustic annotations. Imagery was reported on approximately 82% of listening trials, although its occurrence varied across excerpts. Analyses indicated that subjective appraisals of music and individual imagery ability were associated with imagery occurrence, whereas the broad acoustic components examined did not show a significant direct association. The database also captures variation in the phenomenological characteristics and reported content of imagery experiences through complementary quantitative and qualitative measures. MUSIMAGINE provides an openly accessible resource for examining relationships among music stimuli, listener characteristics, subjective appraisals, and the occurrence and characteristics of MEMI. It offers a foundation for further behavioural, computational, and neuroscientific research, while enabling future studies to test and extend patterns observed in the present dataset.

articles_hidden.title: Examining within-person fluctuations and between-person differences in motivational and control processes associated with momentary and daily alcohol use
articles_hidden.authors: Jennie Lukoff; Ilse H. van de Groep; Reshmi Marhe; Willem-Paul Brinkman; Ingmar Franken; Andrew Jones; Joran Jongerling; Danielle Remmerswaal
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Alcohol use may reflect both intentional processes and failures of self-regulation, yet their relative relevance to everyday drinking remains unclear. Therefore, we examined whether perceived control, planned use, craving, and inhibitory control were associated with alcohol use among regular drinkers at momentary and daily timescales. Methods. A total of 142 regular alcohol users (40 males, 102 females; M = 33.30 years, SD = 14.76) completed a four-day experience sampling method (ESM) study with three daily prompts assessing alcohol use, craving, perceived control, and planned use, directly followed by a mobile Go/No-Go task assessing inhibitory control. Bayesian multilevel models examined whether inhibition errors, planned use, craving, and perceived control were associated with drinking at momentary and daily timescales.
Results. At the momentary level, evidence suggested credible between-person associations between planned use and perceived control and momentary alcohol consumption, and credible negative within-person associations for perceived control and craving. At the daily level, planned use and perceived control showed credible between-person associations with daily alcohol consumption, and females reported lower daily consumption than males. Within-person planned use and inhibition errors were not credible at either level, and no credible within-person associations were found for daily alcohol use.
Conclusions. Perceived control emerged as the most consistent concurrent correlate of alcohol use among regular drinkers at momentary and daily timescales, with planned use emerging as a credible between-person correlate. In contrast, craving and inhibitory control were not robustly associated with drinking. Together, these findings highlight the relevance of perceived control and planned drinking for understanding everyday alcohol use, suggesting that drinking may not simply reflect momentary urges or failures of inhibitory control in regular drinkers. Future research should clarify the temporal and causal relationships among these processes and test whether moments of reduced perceived control represent useful targets for just-in-time interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Parenting Stress and Child Anxiety: Exploring Potential Moderators
articles_hidden.authors: Madison Poisall; Stephanie Estrera; Callie W. Little; Sara Ann Hart
articles_hidden.abstract: Parenting stress, or stress that arises from the demands of parenting, has been linked with children’s internalizing and externalizing behaviors (Rodriguez, 2011; Tsotsi et al., 2019). Of these behaviors, less is known about its unique relation to anxiety, a prevalent and significant disorder for many children. The present study aims to address this gap by examining the relation between parenting stress and childhood anxiety while also testing whether parental psychological distress or child resilience would emerge as significant moderators. Parenting stress was found to positively predict children’s anxiety, such that as parenting stress increases, so does child anxiety. However, neither parental psychological distress nor child resilience emerged as significant moderators of this relation. Future studies should explore other potential variables that could act as risk or resilience factors to further our understanding of factors that may exacerbate or protect against increased child anxiety due to parenting stress.

articles_hidden.title: Nonparametric inference of stability landscapes from intensive longitudinal data
articles_hidden.authors: Jingmeng Cui; Eva Ceulemans; francis tuerlinckx
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychological processes are characterized by constant change and complex underlying dynamics and are often researched using intensive longitudinal data (ILD). Although such data are often analyzed with parametric models, these models impose strong and simplified assumptions about the system’s dynamic rules that can be unrealistic and may fail to capture phenomena such as multistability. Recent work has enabled estimation of the stability landscape of psychological systems from ILD, yet drawing statistical inferences from such landscapes remains challenging. In this work, we present a new method for statistical inference based on stability landscapes. The core of the method is bootstrapping, complemented by specialized techniques applied before and after the bootstrap procedure to make computation feasible and to effectively summarize information across bootstrap samples. Across three simulation studies with different data-generating mechanisms, we evaluated the method and, in particular, four approaches for summarizing information about the locations and depths of local minima. Overall, we found that using fixed reference points, such as the local minima from the original sample, helps guide the assignment of bootstrapped minima. When the data-generating mechanism differs from the estimated stability landscape, directional bias may occur; however, the relative locations of minima can still be retrieved. The method generally shows higher precision, whereas achieving high recall may require clear separation between minima, longer time series, and lower measurement noise. We also provide an empirical illustration using an existing dataset. An implementation is available in the latest version of the R package fitlandr.

articles_hidden.title: Image size effect on memory generalizes to deeper encoding and cannot be explained by perceptual measures
articles_hidden.authors: Shaimaa Masarwa; Olga Kreichman; Sharon Gilaie-Dotan
articles_hidden.abstract: We have recently found that during shallow (“naturalistic”/incidental) encoding larger images are better remembered. However, it is unclear whether this reflects a genuine influence of image size on mnemonic processes or an epiphenomenal consequence of its influence on perception, and whether this effect robustly generalizes to deeper encoding. Here, we tested these in three experiments (n = 189) differing in encoding depth: naturalistic (freely viewing the images without being informed a memory test will follow), intentional memorization (freely viewing while memorizing the images since a memory test was to follow), or perceptual encoding (reporting for each image whether there was a person in it and whether it was taken indoors or outdoors, without being informed a memory test will follow). During encoding in the perceptual experiment, participants viewed 160 images of different sizes (3°-15.5°) followed by an old-new recognition memory test of 320 images (half “old”). While perceptual measures were at ceiling, memory improved with image size, presenting a dissociation between perception and memory and indicating that the effect of image size on memory is not a mere reflection of limited perception for smaller images. Additionally, the effect of image size on memory generalized to all encoding tasks such that memory improved for larger images (as evident by accuracy and d’), regardless of average memory performance increasing with encoding depth. These findings suggest that image size operates as a genuine sensory-based modulator of memory encoding, beyond perceptual sensitivity, pointing to a broader role of low-level visual properties in shaping memory representations.

articles_hidden.title: Effectiveness of Single-Session Interventions (SSIs) for Anxiety and Depression in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Nursima Nas; Metta Rahmadiana; N. de Ponti; Clara Miguel; Davide Papola; Eirini Karyotaki; Jessica L. Schleider; Mathias Harrer; Pim Cuijpers; S.E. Stashower
articles_hidden.abstract:
ABSTRACT
Objective: Single-session interventions (SSIs) have been proposed as a scalable approach to reduce anxiety and depressive symptoms; however, evidence for adults remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating SSIs relative to inactive or minimal-control conditions.
Method: A systematic search identified adult RCTs. Outcomes were analyzed separately for anxiety and depression using three-level random-effects meta-analytic models. Effects were pooled across 1–13 weeks and within short-term (1–3 weeks) and medium-term (4–13 weeks) follow-up windows.
Results: Twenty-one RCTs (N = 7,035) contributed 53 outcome-level effect sizes. Across 1–13 weeks, SSIs were associated with significant reductions in anxiety symptoms (g = −0.66, 95% CI [−0.98, −0.34]) and depressive symptoms (g = −0.49, 95% CI [−0.84, −0.13]). At 1–3 weeks, effects were significant for anxiety symptoms (g = −0.80, 95% CI [−1.24, −0.36]), but not depressive symptoms (g = −0.78, 95% CI [−1.78, 0.22]).
