At 4–13 weeks, effects were significant for both depressive symptoms (g = −0.29, 95% CI [−0.55, −0.02]) and anxiety symptoms (g = −0.48, 95% CI [−0.93, −0.02]). Heterogeneity was high, prediction intervals were wide, publication bias was detected for anxiety outcomes at 1–13 and 1–3 weeks and for depression at 1–13 weeks, and most studies had some concerns or high risk of bias.
Conclusions: SSIs may reduce anxiety and depressive symptoms over the short-to-medium term in adults. Substantial heterogeneity, limited trial availability, publication bias, and risk of bias constrain confidence in the magnitude and generalizability of these effects. Rigorous trials with extended follow-up are needed to clarify effect durability and further inform the role within routine care.

Keywords: anxiety, depression, meta-analysis, single-session interventions, systematic review

articles_hidden.title: Consumer experiences and perceptions of change during psychotherapy for suicide imagery – a mixed-methods case series of Integrated skills for SUicide IMagery (I-SUIM)
articles_hidden.authors: Ann Martin; Demee Rheinberger; Peter McEvoy; Georgie Paulik; William Crompton; Lauren Stavropoulos; Melissa Black; Fiona Shand
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and objectives: This study is the first to explore mechanisms of change and engagement experiences for consumers completing a tailored intervention involving imagery rescripting, replacement implementation intentions, and imagery rehearsal to target hypothesised mechanisms of suicide imagery (Integrated skills for SUicide IMagery; I-SUIM).
Design and Methods: Adult participants with suicide imagery (N = 8) completed two weekly baseline surveys, followed by 3-4 I-SUIM sessions with post-session measures, and a two-week follow-up survey. Evaluation included qualitative interviews at follow-up and mixed-methods surveys collecting qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings of suicide imagery duration, coping, imagery meaning, distress, suicide urge, imagery features, and metacognitions.
Results: No participants dropped out of treatment, and there were no series adverse events. All participants endorsed the intervention as beneficial. Most reported improved understanding of imagery precipitants and function, meaning, and safety plan use. Improvements in other mechanisms were more variable, including changes to imagery features, defusion, emotion changes, and metacognitive shifts. Participants noted some challenges including temporary imagery salience and negative affect immediately following rescripting and difficulty practicing independently. Participants described the role of an experienced and empathetic therapist important to guide intervention and help them feel less alone. 
Limitations: There was no control arm and the study was not designed to demonstrate efficacy.
Conclusions: I-SUIM appears safe and acceptable with qualitatively reported improvements. However, the specific nature of improvements may vary between individuals, and future research is required to assess efficacy across a range of cognitive, emotional, and behavioural outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: A REM Model of Collaborative Recognition Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Yiyan Tan; Richard M. Shiffrin; Timothy J. Pleskac
articles_hidden.abstract: Recognition memory is often studied as an individual process, yet many recognition decisions are made collaboratively. Collaborative recognition requires individuals to communicate and combine separate, imperfect memory evidence to reach a joint decision. Here, we develop a computational model of collaborative recognition memory (CO-REM) grounded in the well-established Retrieving Effectively from Memory (REM) model of individual recognition. We compare collaborative decision rules based on categorical old/new decisions, confidence judgments, and the direct integration of memory evidence. The simulations show that groups can outperform even their best individual member, but the benefits depend on differences in individual recognition ability and how memory evidence is communicated and combined. Confidence sharing can produce collective gains or losses depending on how individuals map their memory evidence onto confidence judgments. The model also predicts greater collaborative benefits for recognizing previously studied items (targets) than for correctly rejecting new items (lures), consistent with some previous empirical findings. Although the predicted performance differences are small, CO-REM provides a framework for identifying the conditions under which collaboration improves recognition and for guiding future empirical investigations.

articles_hidden.title: A Systems Approach to Understanding Experiences of Primary Healthcare in Underserved Autistic Communities: Development and Evaluation of Participatory Creative Systems Mapping
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria Newell; Neil Anderson; Ayman Eckford; Katie Needham; Maggie Scrivener; Alexandra Webster; Vyv Huddy; Rachael Hughson-Gill; Ian Kellar; Joe Langley
articles_hidden.abstract:
Autistic people who are racially minoritised, are from areas of high economic deprivation, have co-occurring learning disabilities, or are non- or minimally-speaking are frequently excluded from autism research. This leaves critical gaps in evidence for service development. We addressed this by developing and evaluating “Participatory Creative Systems Mapping (PCSM)” – an emerging practice that combines Community-Based Participatory Research, Participatory Systems Mapping, and creative methods. The novelty arises from combining these approaches to systemically reduce barriers to underserved autistic communities’ participation and engagement in research.

We partnered with disability-focused and community organisations, and an autistic steering group to develop and deliver accessible workshops. These workshops incorporated persona development, user journey mapping, storyboarding, and live artist visualisation to translate underserved autistic peoples’ experiences of primary healthcare into system-level insights. 

Thirty-one participants (including autistic adults and parents of autistic people) took part across four individual workshops. The participant cohort included representation from Somali and Black African communities (35.5%), areas of high neighbourhood deprivation, and reported a variety of methods for how they usually communicate. Autistic people with learning disabilities were represented, but this was not consistently self-reported by participants. Evaluation indicated high satisfaction, with all respondents who provided feedback about sharing their ideas and experiences reporting that they felt able to do so in the workshops. As proof of concept for PCSM as a method, we successfully produced a causal loop diagram reflected on by the steering group – the "Misalignment-Invalidation Cycle", illustrating how communication barriers and clinician invalidation generate reinforcing loops of misunderstanding and disengagement from healthcare. 

Finally, we share key methodological lessons for trust-building, flexibility, and accessibility infrastructure. These offer a roadmap for researchers who are seeking to engage underserved autistic people in participatory, system-level inquiry.

articles_hidden.title: Depression–Mindfulness Profiles and Transitions among Adolescents Receiving Animal Assisted Group Psychotherapy
articles_hidden.authors: Sonja Kälin; Mascha Molog; Patricia Pendry; Ruslan Leontjevas; Marion Seidel; Christopher Kutschke; Karin Hediger
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and objectives: Adolescents receiving inpatient mental health care differ considerably in their symptom burden, psychological resources, and patterns of change. This study identified latent profiles based on depressive symptoms and mindfulness and examined transitions between these profiles among adolescents participating in animal-assisted group psychotherapy.
Methods: The sample comprised 108 adolescent inpatients aged 12–18 years (M age = 15.84 years, SD = 1.26) who participated in a five-week animal-assisted group psychotherapy program alongside standard inpatient treatment. Depressive symptoms and mindfulness were assessed before and after the intervention using the Beck Depression Inventory–Fast Screen and the Freiburg Mindfulness Inventory. Profiles for each time point were identified using latent profile analysis and linked longitudinally using latent transition analysis.
Results: Three profiles were identified at both measurement points: reduced burden (T1: n = 14, 14.0%; T2: n = 28, 26.7%), characterized by low depressive symptoms and high mindfulness; moderate burden (T1: n = 46, 46.0%; T2: n = 33, 31.4%); and elevated burden (T1: n = 40, 40.0%; T2: n = 44, 41.9%), characterized by high depressive symptoms and low mindfulness. Estimated transition probabilities indicated that 100% of adolescents in the reduced-burden profile and 86.9% of those in the elevated-burden profile at T1 remained in their respective profiles at T2. Among adolescents in the moderate-burden profile at T1, 27.7% transitioned to the reduced-burden profile over the five-week intervention period.
Conclusions: Adolescents showed distinct depression–mindfulness profiles with different patterns of stability and change. Adolescents with moderate initial burden were most likely to transition toward a more favorable profile, suggesting that they may represent a particularly responsive subgroup. These findings highlight heterogeneity in adolescents’ patterns of functioning and change during multimodal inpatient treatment incorporating animal-assisted group psychotherapy.

articles_hidden.title: CogFlow: Open-Source Solution for the Construction of Modular Cognitive Psychology Experiments
articles_hidden.authors: Kamilya Salibayeva; Alexander Thorpe; Sachi Lardner; Ami Eidels; Guy Hawkins
articles_hidden.abstract: Proliferating web-based experimentation platforms have substantially broadened access to cognitive psychology research infrastructure, yet no existing tool simultaneously supports continuous and trial-based paradigms, maintains institutional data-protection compliance, works across online and laboratory settings, and operates within the constraints of collaborative multi-site teams. We present CogFlow, a free, open-source, self-hostable web platform for constructing, deploying, and managing cognitive psychology experiments. CogFlow’s JSON-centric architecture uses a single declarative configuration file to specify both study design and runtime instructions for the Interpreter engine, supporting a broad task library including Random Dot Motion, Flanker, SART, Stroop and Emotional Stroop, Simon, Task Switching, PVT, MOT, N-back, Gabor patch, Continuous Image Presentation, and Security Operations Center (SOC)-style multitask environments, in both trial-based and continuous-presentation modes. A no-code graphical Builder lowers the barrier to experiment authoring while preserving full parameter-level configurability for researchers who require it; results are collected as encrypted payloads with multi-factor authentication gating and pseudonymized participant linkage, supporting compliance with GDPR, UK GDPR, and IRB data management requirements. The platform integrates natively with SONA Systems and Prolific Academic for participant recruitment, provides in-portal descriptive analysis and charting, and includes a CogFlow To Go packaging mode for offline laboratory deployment with Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) support for physiological co-registration. Software-layer runtime benchmarks confirm stable performance consistent with the broader literature on browser-based platforms. CogFlow is available at https://cogflow.app under the BSD 3-Clause license; contributor roles are tracked using the CRediT taxonomy with versioned archival via Zenodo.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental Trajectories and Transitions in Callous-Unemotional Traits Across Adolescence: The Role of Parenting and Emotion Dysregulation
articles_hidden.authors: Rowan C Moore; Dylan G. Gee; Arielle Baskin–Sommers; Rebecca G. Brady
articles_hidden.abstract: Callous-unemotional (CU) traits reflect low empathy, guilt, and concern for others and are associated with persistent antisocial behavior, aggression, and delinquency. Although CU traits vary across adolescence, less is known about factors predicting increases versus decreases in severity. Using four annual assessments spanning early to middle adolescence from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Social Development (ABCD-SD) Study, we characterized CU trajectories using latent class growth analysis and examined changes in CU severity between annual assessments. Logistic regression tested whether parenting and emotion dysregulation prospectively distinguished shifts in CU severity among adolescents who moved between categories. Three developmental trajectories emerged: Low (46.9%), Moderate (40.1%), and Elevated (13.0%). Among adolescents beginning at moderate severity, greater positive parenting was associated with movement to low rather than elevated CU severity (OR = 0.69, p < .001), whereas greater negative parenting (OR = 1.21, p = .024) and emotion dysregulation (OR = 1.18, p = .036) were associated with movement to elevated rather than low severity. Among adolescents beginning at low severity, greater positive parenting was associated with movement to moderate rather than directly to elevated severity (OR = 0.82, p = .045), whereas greater emotion dysregulation was associated with movement directly to elevated rather than moderate severity (OR = 1.37, p = .003). These findings demonstrate that CU trajectories can remain relatively stable at the group level even as adolescents show year-to-year shifts in CU severity, and identify parenting and emotion dysregulation as prospective predictors and potentially modifiable targets for reducing CU traits.

articles_hidden.title: Young children are curious about what others think about them
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Zhu; Carol Dweck; Hyowon Gweon
articles_hidden.abstract: Growing up involves learning about ourselves: Who am I, what can I do, and how can I improve? Although social feedback from knowledgeable others (e.g., parents, teachers) serves as a critical source of information for learning about the self, little work has examined children’s curiosity about this information. Using both naturalistic information-seeking behaviors and a binary choice measure, the current work investigates whether and when preschool-aged children seek in- formation about what others think about them. We find that children are more curious about how an adult evaluated their own drawing compared to a drawing made by an unknown peer, while ruling out possible alternative explanations (Experiments 1–3). Critically, this curiosity was modulated by children’s uncertainty about their performance (Experiment 4), suggesting that children’s preference for the self reflects genuine information-seeking. These findings provide evidence for an early-emerging curiosity about what others think about the self.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Dementia: From Network Degeneration to Compassionate and Skilled Care
articles_hidden.authors: William Goette
articles_hidden.abstract: Dementia is a progressive syndrome characterized by neurodegeneration across distributed brain networks that results in cognitive, behavioral, and functional declines. Conventional psychoeducation provides disease facts and resources but often lacks the mechanistic grounding needed to translate knowledge into durable caregiver skills. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) extends traditional approaches by offering brain-based explanations of symptoms and caregiving challenges, paired with learning principles optimized for stressed learners. This chapter proposes a dementia-specific NIPE framework grounded in network-level neuroscience and cognitive reserve, specifying core content domains across the disease course, delivery structures, and mechanism of efficacy. The chapter synthesizes evidence for effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, cultural adaptation, clinician training, and outcome measurement, presenting NIPE as a pragmatic approach to strengthening person-centered dementia care.

articles_hidden.title: Inconclusive longitudinal associations between violence exposure and adolescent conduct problems: A comment on Swingler et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Based on positive cross-lagged effects in data (N = 357, 51.5% female) from two waves of measurement, Swingler et al. concluded that violence exposure in early adolescence represents a prospective risk factor for conduct problems. However, it is well known that cross-lagged effects may be spurious. We fitted alternative models to data simulated to resemble the data used by Swingler et al. and found discrepant increasing, decreasing, and null effects of violence exposure on subsequent change in conduct problems depending on the analyzed model. A meta-analytic pooling of these discrepant effects did not differ significantly from zero. Hence, the findings by Swingler et al. may have been spurious and their conclusion premature. It is important for researchers to bear in mind that associations, including cross-lagged regression effects, in observational (i.e., non-experimental) data may be spurious in order not to overinterpret findings. We recommend researchers to scrutinize cross-lagged effects by fitting alternative models to data and to base conclusions on a juxtaposition of findings.

articles_hidden.title: Introducing the “ASCENT” EEGLAB Plugin: Aperiodic Signal Complexity Estimation for Neurophysiological Time Series
articles_hidden.authors: Cedric Cannard; Arnaud Delorme
articles_hidden.abstract: Entropy- and complexity-based measures are promising tools to characterize neural dynamics beyond traditional linear and oscillatory analyses. However, their adoption in electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) research has been limited by methodological fragmentation, computational cost, and a lack of standardized implementations and visualization tools. Hence, we developed ASCENT, an open-source EEGLAB plugin for computing and visualizing a broad range of entropy, fractal, and aperiodic measures in neurophysiological time series. ASCENT integrates established single-scale, multiscale, and multivariate entropy algorithms, fractal dimension estimators, and aperiodic spectral parameterization within an optimized framework, accessible through both a graphical interface and a fully parameter-tunable command-line interface. To our knowledge, it is the first toolbox to combine these measures on independent component (IC) time series and on scalp channels, and to offer time-resolved estimation of both modified multiscale entropy and aperiodic parameters. Outputs are stored in a structured format for statistical analysis with external tools, as illustrated by an accompanying group-analysis script. As a usage example, we applied ASCENT to resting-state EEG from 40 participants recorded with eyes closed and eyes open. Condition differences were found for multiple measures and temporal scales. Their direction, spatial distribution, and scale extent depended on the measure, the coarse-graining operator and, for the power spectrum, aperiodic correction. Correlation analyses helped to indicate which measures were redundant. ASCENT aims to lower the threshold for researchers to apply these measures consistently and interpret them appropriately.

articles_hidden.title: A Brief Need-Supportive Manipulation and Subsequent Task Performance: A Randomized Experiment
articles_hidden.authors: Chen Erez; Leo Wolmer
articles_hidden.abstract: Within self-determination theory, basic psychological need theory proposes that social environments supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness foster autonomous motivation, engagement, well-being, and effective functioning. Yet experimental evidence that a brief need-supportive context affects subsequent behavioral performance remains limited. In a randomized experiment, psychology undergraduates (N = 121) completed two trials of a timed word-generation task used as a behavioral performance proxy. Between trials, they received an experimenter-delivered multicomponent scripted manipulation intended to support or thwart these needs or a neutral interaction, followed by a stress induction manipulation. In an analysis of covariance with HC3 standard errors, condition predicted Trial 2 performance after adjustment for Trial 1. Participants assigned to the need-supportive condition scored higher than those in the neutral control. The thwarting-control estimate was small and imprecise. A brief need-supportive context may therefore carry over to performance on a subsequent task, conditional on initial performance. Because the manipulation also varied feedback, expectancy, warmth, and contact, the finding is preliminary and does not isolate need support as the operative mechanism.

articles_hidden.title: Development and description of Peers Actively Involved in Rehabilitation (PAIR): A co-designed peer support program for people with acquired brain injury
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Schmidt; Janna Griffioen; Jade Abigail Witten; Adele Rogers; Nanaimo Brain Injury Society; Janelle Breese Biagioni
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Acquired brain injury (ABI) is a leading cause of long term disability in adults. In Canada, while advances in acute care and inpatient rehabilitation have improved survival, many people living with ABI experience persistent challenges following discharge. This can include reduced self efficacy, mental health difficulties, and decreased participation in daily life. Community based supports remain fragmented and difficult to access. Peer support, or mentorship provided by people with lived experience of ABI, has shown promise in improving outcomes in neurological and chronic conditions. However, peer support interventions for ABI are rarely described in sufficient detail to enable replication or implementation.
Objective. To describe the development, theoretical foundations, core components, and delivery of Peers Actively Involved in Rehabilitation (PAIR), a structured, community based peer support intervention for adults living with ABI.
Methods. This paper provides a detailed description of PAIR using the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR), informed by principles from the Guidance for Reporting Intervention Development studies (GUIDED). Data sources include co creation with people with lived experience and community partners, feasibility research, intervention manuals, and operational procedures.
Discussion. PAIR integrates lived experience knowledge into rehabilitation through structured peer support worker training, individualized matching, and flexible delivery embedded within community organizations. By transparently documenting development and delivery, this paper supports replication, adaptation, and future evaluation, and contributes to strengthening person centred, community based rehabilitation for adults living with ABI.

articles_hidden.title: Inconclusive evidence for necessity effects of basic psychological need satisfaction on employee well-being: Re-examining Ding et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Filippa Folke; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Using Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), Ding et al. concluded that employees must experience sufficient satisfaction of their basic psychological needs at work in order to attain high levels of well-being. However, necessity effects obtained with NCA can emerge even in the absence of genuine necessity relations because correlations between variables may create similar patterns. In the present study, we reanalyzed the findings reported by Ding et al. by comparing the observed necessity effects with benchmark values expected from correlation alone. Most of the reported effects (96.4%) were located within or below the estimated ranges of spuriousness, indicating that they were no larger than would be expected under conditions where no true necessity mechanism exists. Consequently, the results reported by Ding et al. provide little support for the conclusion that psychological need satisfaction constitutes a necessary condition for employee well-being. We argue that applications of NCA should routinely incorporate assessments of ranges of spuriousness and that necessity claims should be restricted to effects that clearly exceed these ranges.

articles_hidden.title: Psychiatric Symptom Severity and Performance Monitoring:  Intraindividual Variability in Neural Responses and Behavioral Adjustments to Errors
articles_hidden.authors: Bohyun Park; Scott Baldwin; Michael J. Larson; Peter E Clayson
articles_hidden.abstract: Performance monitoring involves evaluating actions and adjusting behavior accordingly. Atypical neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring are commonly observed in individuals with psychopathology, raising the possibility that psychiatric symptoms may disrupt the link between error-related neural activity and subsequent behavioral adjustment. However, neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring are often examined separately, leaving trial-level event-related brain potential (ERP) coupling with behavior poorly understood. The present study examined whether previous-trial error-related ERP components predicted current-trial behavior (i.e., response time [RT], accuracy) and whether these relationships varied by self-reported internalizing and externalizing symptoms. In a college student sample (N=247), larger previous-trial error-related negativity (ERN), an index of early error monitoring, predicted longer RTs. In contrast, larger previous-trial error positivity (Pe), an index of later error awareness, predicted higher current-trial accuracy. Internalizing and externalizing symptom scores did not robustly moderate these ERP-behavior relationships or consistently predict behavioral adjustments. These findings suggest that trial-level coupling between error-related ERP components and behavioral adjustment showed no robust evidence of differing across levels of self-reported internalizing and externalizing symptoms within the observed range. More broadly, the results highlight the value of examining performance monitoring as an integrated neural-behavioral process rather than as isolated neural or behavioral indices.

articles_hidden.title: How Past Experiences Shape New Beliefs: Generalisation and Adaptation in Human Reinforcement Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Phoenix Pavlik; Tin Nok Isaac Choy; Marko Dimitrovski; Toby Wise
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans are adept at learning under uncertainty. However, the way in which we learn must adapt to different environments, and we must determine when to generalise learning strategies across different contexts, making use of prior experience to guide present learning. However, how learning adapts based on prior experience remains poorly understood. Here, we examine how prior exposure to environments with differing levels of uncertainty shapes subsequent learning. A large sample recruited online (N=330) completed a gamified two-armed bandit task comprising two blocks with varying uncertainty, manipulated through the volatility or changeability of outcome contingencies. Computational modelling enabled the extraction of learning rate parameters quantifying the speed with which participants update their expectations. Analyses revealed significant effects of both previously experienced and current block volatility learning rates, and that this combination of generalisation and adaptation was consistent across learning from positive and negative prediction errors. Exploratory regression and factor analyses did not identify any moderating effects of mental health symptoms. Our results demonstrate that prior experience biases belief updating strategies across environments, revealing a mechanism through which learning both adapts and generalises to facilitate effective behaviour.

articles_hidden.title: Identifying clinically relevant anhedonia in young people aged 16–25: a provisional screening threshold for the Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Sena Demir-Kassem; Katie Prizeman; Ciara McCabe
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Anhedonia is a core symptom of depression and is associated with greater illness severity and poorer outcomes in young people. The Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) is a validated 14-item multidimensional measure, but no empirically derived screening threshold exists for the original English-language scale.
Aims
To derive a provisional ASA screening threshold in older adolescents and young adults.
Method
In 1199 participants aged 16–25 years recruited in the UK, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses evaluated the ASA against three reference criteria: depressive symptom caseness (Mood and Feelings Questionnaire [MFQ] ≥27), self-reported clinician diagnosis of depression (n = 709) and anhedonia caseness on the Snaith–Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS; n = 433). Optimal thresholds were identified using the Youden index, and performance was compared across age groups and gender and in a 5-month follow-up subsample (n = 332).
Results
The ASA had excellent discrimination against MFQ caseness (AUC = 0.89, 95% CI 0.87–0.91; optimal threshold 16.5, sensitivity 86%, specificity 77%). Optimal thresholds were 15.5 against both clinician diagnosis (AUC = 0.74, 95% CI 0.70–0.79; sensitivity 88%, specificity 47%) and SHAPS caseness (AUC = 0.83, 95% CI 0.79–0.87). Discrimination did not differ by age group or gender. At follow-up, discrimination was outstanding (AUC = 0.94, 95% CI 0.91–0.96), although the optimal threshold was higher (19.5).
Conclusions
Thresholds converged at 15.5–16.5 across reference criteria, supporting a provisional screening threshold of ≥17 for identifying clinically relevant anhedonia in young people. Replication against structured clinical assessment is needed before this threshold is used diagnostically.

articles_hidden.title: Choosing isn’t always a walk in the park: Dog food preference versus choice
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Espinosa; Madeline Helmer Pelgrim; Daphna Buchsbaum
articles_hidden.abstract: Preferences underpin a range of fitness behaviors for many mammals such as foraging, object interactions, and even social relationships. Despite the ubiquity of domestic dogs in modern culture, the basis for preferences driving their behavior and choices are not well understood. Past work has found that dogs perceive and respond to certain characteristics of items, specifically an object's familiarity and quality when making choices. However, in the real world, these characteristics don't exist in isolation, and understanding the interaction between familiarity and valuation as they relate to object choice can provide insight into how dogs make decisions. We aimed to explore how item familiarity and quality intersect to form dogs’ preferences for one food over another in a series of two-alternative forced choice tasks. Over three studies, dogs (N = 125) were presented with a classic preference test between two items of unequal quality (Study 1), systematic pairings of four items that contrasted familiarity and quality (Study 2), and aggregates of two items of unequal quality (Study 3). Overall, we found that dogs' choices were driven only by the quality of the food item, and the prior familiarity of the item did not impact choice behavior. Determining what motivates dogs and contributes to their preferences has implications for understanding decision-making at large, as well as for advancing canine science.

articles_hidden.title: Changes in Disordered Eating Across Pregnancy: A Rapid Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Pung; Samah Ellithi; Nurya Toche Mbah; Laurie Charest; Sarah Elizabeth Racine; Anna L. MacKinnon
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives

Disordered eating (DE) can be particularly concerning during pregnancy, as it is associated with various obstetric complications. Findings on DE variations during pregnancy have yet to be systematically synthesized. This review seeks to summarize research on DE change across pregnancy. 

Methods

Four databases were searched using PRISMA Scoping Review and Cochrane Rapid Reviews guidelines. Eligible studies were longitudinal and assessed DE, including eating disorder (ED) symptoms (e.g., dieting, purging) and related forms of DE (e.g., emotional eating), more than once during pregnancy. 

Results

The review included 19 articles. Though many forms of DE decreased across pregnancy, some forms of DE did not change, while some forms of DE had conflicting or unclear patterns. Body image constructs were the most examined forms of DE in pregnancy, followed by weight and dieting constructs. Research comparing DE patterns in people with versus without EDs was scarce.

Conclusions

Few studies have examined DE across pregnancy using ED samples, and several DE symptoms had conflicting or unclear patterns across pregnancy. Moreover, some DE outcomes (e.g., quality of life related to EDs, guilt related to overeating, susceptibility to hunger) and the comparison of DE patterns in samples with versus without EDs remain underexplored in pregnancy.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Psychological Scales with Gold-Standard Items: Lessons from Measures of Body Height, Weight, and Age
articles_hidden.authors: Kathryn Eichhorn; Sven Hilbert; Florian Pargent; Markus Bühner; Janika Saretzki; Jonas Hauck; Larissa Sust
articles_hidden.abstract: This article investigates whether gold-standard items are helpful for questionnaire development. Based on an initial item pool (138 items) derived through a deductive item construction (𝑁 = 124) and a prototype approach (𝑁 = 24), followed by cognitive interviews (𝑁 = 8) and a pilot study (𝑁 = 390) of a preliminary item set (61 items), three 12-item scales were constructed to measure the physical traits of body height, body weight, and age. We collected data on these scales using response formats with either two (𝑁 = 921) or six (𝑁 = 933) categories. We also collected numeric self-reports of body weight, body height, and age as gold-standard items. We argue that the items intended to measure the latent variable (i.e., body height, body weight, age) most directly (i.e., the gold-standard items) should have the highest loadings on that variable. Contrary to this assumption, confirmatory factor analyses revealed that the gold-standard items did not consistently exhibit the highest loadings on their corresponding latent variables, calling into question the content validity of our scales. Furthermore, when controlling for the self-reported physical body height, body weight, and age as gold-standard items, as well as gender, we did not always find an interpretable, systematic residual variance. Finally, the pattern of correlations among the latent variables did not closely reflect those among the self-reported gold-standard items, suggesting that the item scales and the gold-standard items do not share the same validity. While these results are consistent with previous studies, our analyses also showed that items with two response categories were as valid as those with six categories, contradicting past recommendations. Our analyses underscore the importance of intensive cognitive pretesting in scale construction and suggest that questionnaires using different response formats should be compared empirically and that hypotheses about which items best represent the latent variable should be tested.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Attention on Speech Entrainment in Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis Individuals
articles_hidden.authors: Victoria R Poulton; Tineke Grent-'T-Jong; Marion Brickwedde; joachim gross; Christoph U. Correll; Peter J. Uhlhaas
articles_hidden.abstract: Language comprehension is disrupted in schizophrenia and early-stage psychosis, but the contributions of bottom-up and top-down processing remain unclear. In the current electroencephalography (EEG) study, we investigated speech entrainment in a sample of n=21 individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P) and n=25 healthy controls (HCs). Continuous speech was presented through an audiobook in three listening conditions: (1) “Active”, in which participants attended to speech; (2) “Passive”, in which participants passively listened to the audiobook while performing a concurrent visual Flanker task; and (3) “Passive-reversed”, in which participants listened to an unintelligible time-reversed and noise-vocoded version of the audiobook while performing the Flanker task. Mutual Information (MI) analyses were used to assess shared information between the speech amplitude envelope and neural oscillations in the delta (0.25-3 Hz), theta (4.5-6.5 Hz), and alpha (7-10 Hz) frequency ranges. Sensor-level and source-level results indicate stronger delta entrainment in the Active vs. Passive conditions across groups. However, compared to controls, CHR-Ps showed reduced theta entrainment in auditory cortices, independent of condition, and decreased alpha entrainment in the Passive vs. Active condition. The findings point to theta entrainment deficits in CHR-Ps during continuous speech processing, indexing a bottom-up impairment. In contrast, delta and alpha entrainment in CHR-Ps were modulated by attention. Together, these findings highlight that both bottom-up and top-down impairments contribute to speech entrainment deficits in CHR-Ps.

articles_hidden.title: A Qualitative Study of Reproductive Decision-Making Among People with Lived Experience of Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Davies; Claire Wilson; Helena Zavos; Catherine Jones
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a cyclical hormone-related condition, causing significant mood symptoms in the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. Despite the substantial impact it can have on daily life, little is known about how it shapes reproductive decision-making. This study explored how people with PMDD experience and reflect on reproductive decisions, and the role of healthcare support in this. 

Design: Semi-structured qualitative interviews, informed by a feminist critical realist approach.  

Methods: Twenty UK-based adults who had received a diagnosis of, or self-identified as having, PMDD took part. Semi-structured interviews explored experiences of how, if at all, PMDD had impacted thoughts and decisions around pregnancy or parenthood. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, supported by a lived experience advisory group.  

Results: Four themes were developed: PMDD as a whole-family experience; intergenerational awareness and responsibility; assessing readiness and capacity for parenthood; and self-advocacy and negotiating an unsupportive system. Participants not only spoke about how PMDD symptoms shaped their decision-making, but also considered relational impact, the potential heritability of PMDD, and the limited healthcare support available. Support from loved ones, familiarity with their own symptom patterns and establishing strategies for managing PMDD were often described as facilitators of decision-making. Across themes, findings were interpreted within a “good mother” ideal, helping to explain why reproductive decisions often carried emotional and moral weight. 

Conclusions: PMDD can shape reproductive decision-making in complex ways. Findings demonstrate the need for PMDD-specific support that helps people make informed decisions aligned with their circumstances and needs.

articles_hidden.title: Interpersonal Processes in Daily Life: Loneliness and Social Appraisals as Real-Time Predictors of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Urges and Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle Katherine Hiner; Laurence Claes; Brooke A. Ammerman; Olivia J Kirtley; Julie Janssens; Inez Myin-Germeys; Glenn Kiekens
articles_hidden.abstract: Although interpersonal factors are implicated in theoretical models of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), little is known about how objective social context and subjective interpersonal experiences contribute to momentary NSSI urges and behaviors in clinical populations. The present study examined between- and within-person associations among several interpersonal processes (perceived rejection, perceived social support, social context, social context appraisals, loneliness) and NSSI urges and behavior in daily life. One-hundred-twenty-five treatment-seeking adolescents and adults with recent NSSI completed a 28-day Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) protocol with six daily surveys (15,098 assessments). Dynamic structural equation modeling examined between- and within-person contemporaneous and temporal associations. Higher perceived rejection at baseline predicted greater average NSSI urge intensity and NSSI behavior during the 28-day EMA period, whereas baseline perceived social support was unrelated to either outcome. Momentary objective social context (i.e., being alone versus with others) was not a robust predictor of NSSI urges or behavior in daily life. In contrast, more positive momentary appraisals of social contexts predicted prospective decreases in NSSI urge intensity across 2-hour intervals, while higher-than-usual momentary loneliness predicted within-person increases in both NSSI urge intensity and the likelihood of NSSI behavior. Fully prospective mediation analyses indicated that the temporal effects of loneliness and social context appraisals on NSSI behavior operated primarily through their effect on NSSI urges. Subjective interpersonal experiences, rather than objective social context, were consistently linked to short-term NSSI risk. Interventions targeting maladaptive social appraisals and loneliness, including just-in-time adaptive interventions, may help prevent NSSI urges and behavior in daily life.

articles_hidden.title: The dimensionality and influence of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism in Nordfriesland and Fryslân
articles_hidden.authors: Ruth Kircher; Suzanne Victoria Dekker; Jelske Dijkstra; Pavlina Heinzova; Mirjam Vellinga
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism in the district of Nordfriesland, Germany, and the province of Fryslân, the Netherlands. Both are home to speakers of the local majority language (i.e. German/Dutch), autochthonous heritage languages (e.g. Frisian), and immigrant heritage languages (e.g. Arabic). Quantitative questionnaire data were collected from 645 parents of young children, making this the first large-scale study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism outside Québec. There were three key findings. First, like in Québec, three evaluative dimensions emerged from parents’ attitudes: status, solidarity, and cognitive development – indicating that these dimensions may characterise parental attitudes across contexts. Second, parents with more positive solidarity-related attitudes were more likely to raise their children multilingually in the home. This is the first time a significant relationship between parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism and multilingual child-rearing in the home has been attested. Third, no significant attitudinal differences were found between parents in Nordfriesland and Fryslân. The study makes a theoretical contribution by advancing knowledge relevant to attitude theory, and a practical contribution by serving as a basis for research-informed science communication for policy makers and language planners wishing to promote multilingual child-rearing and intergenerational heritage language transmission.

articles_hidden.title: Consensus without a champion: Cross-partisan demand for AI safety regulation in Hungary and the missing belief in delivery
articles_hidden.authors: Gabor Orosz; Janos Salamon; Reza Shabahang; Agnes Zsila; Péter Krekó
articles_hidden.abstract: Industry leaders now ask for independent, pre-release safety testing of frontier AI systems; the US president dismissed such calls as fears about things that “won’t happen.” What the public wants is well documented for the US and UK, but almost unknown elsewhere, and little is known about whether people believe their preference will be acted upon. In a Hungarian online sample (n = 1,356), 75% supported mandatory independent safety testing before AI systems are released, regardless of partisanship. Three in four also believed most Hungarians agree, and 61% believed that this majority was growing. Yet only 32% expected such testing to be introduced. In one of Europe’s most polarized countries, AI safety regulation thus has a consensus but no champion. The missing link is not a hidden majority but the belief that anyone will deliver it.

articles_hidden.title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Cognitive Bias Modification for Interpretation in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Tönsing; Marcel Miché; Johannes Massell; Roselind Lieb; Karina Wahl
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Cognitive bias modification for interpretation directly modifies maladaptive interpretation biases, central to the development and maintenance of obsessive-compulsive disorder. Although it has been examined across a range of disorders, its efficacy for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) has not been synthesized.

Methods: A systematic search of Embase, PubMed, and PsycInfo (last search 5 May 2026) identified randomized controlled studies targeted OCD-relevant interpretation biases. The synthesis combines a narrative mapping of design and training parameters, followed by three random-effects meta-analyses for interpretation biases, OCD-relevant beliefs, and OCD symptom severity. Prespecified moderators were training dosage, targeted domain, control condition, and study sample. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty of evidence with GRADE. The review was preregistered (https://osf.io/n3hbk).

Results: Across 19 studies (N = 1,294), single-session designs predominated in analogue samples and multi-session protocols in the few clinical studies. Cognitive bias modification for interpretation showed a large effect on interpretation biases (g = -0.92 [-1.18, -0.65]), a moderate effect on OCD-relevant beliefs (g = -0.40 [-0.57, -0.22]), and a small effect on OCD symptom severity (g = -0.19 [-0.34, -0.04]). General or mixed training protocols outperformed domain-specific protocols, and symptom reductions were larger in clinical than in subclinical samples. All studies raised some concerns on RoB 2, and certainty of evidence ranged from low to moderate.

Conclusions: We present empirical evidence that cognitive bias modification for interpretation reliably modifies post-intervention interpretation biases, with moderate transfer to OCD-relevant beliefs and small transfer effects on OCD symptom severity, supporting its potential as an adjunctive intervention. The larger effects observed for broader training protocols and in clinical samples highlight that future trials should prioritize clinical samples, multi-session designs, preregistration, and outcome measures that are independent of the training paradigm. Given the few studies per subgroup these findings require replication.

articles_hidden.title: Breaking the Stasis in the Polyvagal Controversy: Two Category Errors, a Missing Variable, and a Measured Boundary
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriel Kram; Heather MacDuffie
articles_hidden.abstract: For twenty years, the dispute over Polyvagal Theory (PVT) has turned on whether the profound bradycardia attributed to dorsal vagal shutdown occurs in ordinary human freezing and dissociation. The 2026 Grossman–Porges exchange sharpened that dispute without resolving it. We argue that it cannot be resolved as framed, because neither position specifies the variable that would adjudicate it: the pervading neurochemistry under which a recruited circuit operates. PVT made the required observation once, in 2001, when it paired oxytocin-conditioned calm immobilization with vasopressin-conditioned immobilized fear at identical dorsal vagal anatomy. The observation was never generalized, because the neurochemical model PVT inherits retains a two-pole structure in which the endogenous opioids have no position. We propose a three-variable model in which neuroception selects the circuitry recruited and modulatory chemistry determines what that circuitry produces. As a falsifiable hypothesis, severable from the model, we propose that the cardiac and respiratory signature of life-threat immobilization requires endogenous µ-opioid activity, and that naloxone administered during confirmed shutdown should reverse bradycardia and restore respiration on the timescale of the drug’s onset. Independently of the model, electron-microscopic fiber counts of human vagal tissue show that the supradiaphragmatic/subdiaphragmatic discontinuity is confined to the myelinated population, placing that partition on direct measurement rather than comparative inference. Because escapability rather than phylogenetic age selects the state, PVT’s clinical claims do not depend on its evolutionary reconstruction. The observations of both parties describe physiologically distinct conditions, and the model, drawn from Autonomics, converts a twenty-year standoff into experimentally decidable predictions.

articles_hidden.title: Hidden Neural Variability and the Unexplained Cochlear Implant Outcome
articles_hidden.authors: Kuzma Strelnikov
articles_hidden.abstract: Cochlear implants work, but not equally. After decades of cohort studies, the familiar predictors of outcome (age, duration of deafness, residual hearing, etiology) still leave most of the spread between patients unexplained. Research on how the brain handles degraded speech, audiovisual cues and everyday sounds shows that implant outcome measures test the brain at least as much as the ear. Yet candidacy assessment still examines the cochlea, the auditory nerve and inner-ear anatomy, and rarely the cognitive and structural state of the brain that must learn to use the device. This article argues that undetected neural variability, including cognitive decline, hearing-related atrophy and incidental pathology in brains assumed to be normal, is a plausible and largely unmeasured contributor to the missing variance. It proposes routine cognitive and volumetric phenotyping of implant candidates, and of the control groups against which they are judged. Because the brain restores much of the degraded implant signal through its predictive mechanisms, the article also calls for a new line of work: the development of dedicated tests of predictive brain capacity, a measure currently absent from both candidacy assessment and outcome research.

articles_hidden.title: The orthoblique rotation for factor analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Marcos Jiménez; Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal; Víthor Rosa Franco; Luis Eduardo Garrido; Francisco José Abad
articles_hidden.abstract: The gradient projection algorithm (GPA) is the most used tool to rotate factor models. However, GPA is currently limited to fully orthogonal or fully oblique solutions. Keeping structural zeros in selected positions of the factor correlation matrix after rotation is currently unavailable. This limitation is relevant to analyses where theoretical considerations or study design require certain factor correlations to be zero. We therefore introduce the orthoblique rotation, which allows orthogonal and oblique relations between factors to coexist. Building on Jennrich's algorithms, we describe the geometric foundations of GPA and extend them to the orthoblique rotation. We illustrate its usefulness for exploratory bifactor models with multiple correlated general factors that remain orthogonal to group factors, and for multitrait–multimethod models in which trait and method factors may correlate within their respective sets while remaining orthogonal between sets. Finally, we make available the new orthoblique rotation in the R package latent through the lrotate() function, which extends the capabilities of the popular GPArotation package of Bernaards and Jennrich (2005). Taken together, this work helps bridge the gap between exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and continues Jennrich's efforts to expand the flexibility and scope of factor rotation.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Sleep Disorders in Psychiatry
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammad Nami
articles_hidden.abstract: Sleep disorders are prevalent among psychiatric patients and are strongly associated with neurobiological, psychological, and behavioral processes. This chapter analyzes neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE), an approach incorporating the insights gained from neuroscience with patient education to understand and manage sleep disturbances better. To establish a scientific basis for psychoeducational interventions, we discuss central mechanisms of sleep regulation such as circadian rhythms, sleep homeostasis, neurotransmitter systems, and brain networks. It illustrates how bidirectional sleep disorders and psychiatric syndromes, including depression, anxiety, PTSD, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), are linked, and explains sleep disturbance as a transdiagnostic key clinical feature. In addition to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, NIPE is used to provide a solution to insomnia by integrating mindfulness-based strategies and personalized interventions with the assistance of digital technologies. Implementation challenges and outcome assessment, as well as ethical dimensions of practice, are also considered. In fact, NIPE is a clinically relevant strategy that can both maximize patient engagement and ameliorate sleep disorder outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Behavioral Adaptation: Evaluating the Added Value of EEG in Personalized Language Interfaces
articles_hidden.authors: João Fernandes; Carlos Bruno; Luis Ricardo Santos
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuroadaptive interfaces personalize human–computer interaction using brain activity, but whether neural measurements provide useful information beyond behavioral indicators remains unclear, particularly in language comprehension tasks. We propose a framework to investigate the added value of EEG in adaptive communication support. Written messages are presented through combinations of sentence segmentation, pictograms, and keyword labels, with presentation choices informed by individual preferences and task performance. A behavior-adaptive policy serves as the baseline for comparison with a neuroadaptive policy incorporating calibrated EEG estimates under signal-quality and uncertainty constraints. The research plan includes interface validation, behavioral feasibility testing, and an EEG-based comparison using held-out sessions. Evaluation focuses on comprehension accuracy, response time, subjective effort, and adaptation behavior. The objective is to determine whether neural information improves assistance decisions and user outcomes beyond behavioral adaptation.

articles_hidden.title: Moralised Essentialism and Identity Closure in Moral Character Judgement
articles_hidden.authors: Emile Boullineau
articles_hidden.abstract: Accepting an excuse lowers blame, but whether it changes what observers think of the person is unsettled. An excuse admits an act was wrong but pleads reduced responsibility. Read as folk psychology, character accounts of excuse imply that an excuse making an act less revealing should soften judgement of the person. Moralised Essentialism predicts otherwise. Its central rule, identity closure, holds that once a wrong is taken to reveal who the actor is, excuses explain the act and reduce blame but leave the view of the person unchanged. The claim is that excuses stop reaching that judgement, not that they carry less weight. As excuses strengthen, observers should attribute the act more to the situation and blame less, while their judgements of who the actor is, and their forecasts of the actor’s conduct elsewhere, barely move. Retraction and reinterpretation, unlike excuses, change what the act was and should lower those judgements, which strict belief perseverance denies. A proposed experiment fixes two tests beforehand. Meaningful revision of those judgements under excuses observers credit as mitigating would reject the account. Judgements that hold or rise after accepted retraction or reinterpretation would reject closure as the explanation of their stability under excuses.

articles_hidden.title: Neutral minus neutral: Liminal spaces as an uncanny phenomenon of unexplained human absence
articles_hidden.authors: Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: Photographs of empty corridors and commercial facilities, known online as "liminal spaces," are judged uncanny by many online viewers. Because most theories of uncanniness locate its cause in the features of humans depicted in the photograph, the appreciation of images that contain no human or animal figures can be used to investigate whether this impression requires a depicted human or whether the expectation that people should be present is sufficient. In a previous empirical study of liminal images, images of rooms from which furniture, doors, and windows had been removed were rated as more than twice as uncanny as the corresponding typical rooms. The effect of human absence, however, has been examined only by replacing human figures with furniture of the same size. Each of four existing accounts, including the structural deviation account, which attributes the impression to deviation from a familiar configuration, explains, on its own, only part of the findings of that study. Here we propose a four-stage model in which uncanniness arises when an observer who judges a place to be in use cannot find a reason for the absence of people or objects that should be there. On the basis of the model, we specify five issues to be tested empirically on which the model and existing accounts make different predictions.

articles_hidden.title: When Unusual Is Usual:  Multivariate Analysis of WAIS-5 Index Score Profiles
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Skirrow
articles_hidden.abstract:
Interpretation of cognitive profiles commonly involves the identification of low scores, discrepancies and relative strengths and weaknesses. However, a finding that is unusual when considered individually may be considerably less unusual within a person's broader cognitive profile. To account for this, Crawford et al. (2012) developed a multivariate approach that placed individual WAIS-IV findings within their wider normative context. The present study extends this approach to the five primary indices of the WAIS-5. 
Monte Carlo simulation of 1,000,000 normative profiles was used to estimate base rates for four complementary aspects of profile interpretation: the rarity of the overall index-score configuration using the Mahalanobis Distance Index (MDI), multiple low index scores, multiple unusual pairwise discrepancies, and multiple relative strengths and weaknesses. Individually unusual findings occurred substantially more frequently when considered across the complete profile, particularly for pairwise discrepancies, where ten overlapping comparisons are possible. The MDI provided complementary information about the rarity of the complete five-index configuration and was more strongly associated with within-profile variability than with overall score level. Together with the accompanying clinical calculator, these analyses provide an accessible framework for placing individual findings and broader patterns of WAIS-5 performance within their normative context.

articles_hidden.title: Healing campuses: Implementing Nature-Based Interventions to Promote University Student Mental Health and Wellbeing
articles_hidden.authors: Melissa O’Shea; Brittany Patafio; David Skvarc; Cindy Zhou; hannah capon; Tracy Garvin; Nina Hunter; Claire Henderson-Wilson; Justin T Lawson; Dieter Kotte
articles_hidden.abstract: Innovative and accessible strategies are needed to address mental health burden among university students. Nature-based interventions (NBIs), which involve therapeutic activities conducted in nature spaces, are emerging to promote student wellbeing on university campuses. This review examined the range of NBIs implemented within universities and their reported benefits using a systematic search and narrative synthesis methodology. Evidence was searched from database inception to August 2026, identifying twelve studies representing eleven trials across five countries. Interventions involved forest therapy (n=5), mindfulness-based programs (n=4) adapted for outdoor campus settings, and therapeutic horticulture interventions (n=3). Evidence suggests that forest therapy is associated with reductions in stress and anxiety and improvements in mood, attention and overall wellbeing. Nature-integrated mindfulness programs were linked to reduced depressive symptoms, rumination, stress and anxiety, alongside enhanced wellbeing, mindfulness and connection to nature. Preliminary evidence suggests on campus therapeutic horticulture interventions may be associated with improvements in anxiety among university students and represent an accessible and affordable way to build nature and social connection. While findings are promising, evidence remains limited and of weak quality, highlighting the need for further robust research on implementation and sustainability within university contexts.

articles_hidden.title: From defeat to entrapment—and back again: Reciprocal dynamics among constructs from the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model of suicide in young adults
articles_hidden.authors: Neha Parvez; Michael Kyron; Emilia Sherifi; Jeremy Gordon Stewart
articles_hidden.abstract: The Integrated Motivational-Volitional (IMV) model of suicide proposes that feelings of defeat give rise to entrapment, which in turn contributes to suicidal ideation (SI). Although research generally supports this pathway, less is understood about how defeat, entrapment, and SI mutually influence each other over short periods of time. Within a three-week ecological momentary assessment period, we examined short-term temporal associations among defeat, entrapment, and SI (passive and active) in a sample of young adults (N = 156, ages 18-29; data collected 2022-2023) with a recent history of suicidal thoughts or behaviours. We used residual dynamic structural equation models to test concurrent and prospective within-person associations among variables. Higher-than-usual levels of defeat and entrapment were each associated with greater passive and active SI at the same assessment and predicted greater SI at the subsequent assessment. Defeat and entrapment also demonstrated reciprocal associations over time, such that greater levels of each predicted subsequent increases in the other. Similarly, higher-than-usual levels of passive SI predicted subsequent increases in both defeat and entrapment, whereas active SI predicted subsequent increases in defeat only. Findings support the central role of defeat and entrapment in short-term changes in SI. Further, they suggest that the relationship between defeat and entrapment may be reciprocal rather than strictly unidirectional, challenging assumptions of the IMV model. The generalizability of these findings to other age groups and clinical populations remains to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Adolescent Perspectives on Parental Consent Requirements for Depression Treatment: A Mixed-Methods Investigation
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda Smock; Tubanji Walubita; Andy Rapoport; Shannon Hill; Aileen Kangavary; Riley McDanal; Mallory Dobias; Juan Pablo Zapata; Briana Shiri Last; Jessica L. Schleider
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression incidence in adolescents is increasing, yet most do not access treatment. Policies requiring parental consent to initiate care may influence adolescent treatment access. In a convergent mixed methods study, we investigated adolescent perspectives toward accessing treatment with and without parental consent (i.e., self-consent) across four modalities: therapy (in-person and online) and self-guided supports (in-person and online). We explored differences in attitudes amongst sub-samples, demographics, and depression severity. An online survey and qualitative interviews were conducted with 43 adolescents; one sub-sample required parental consent (n = 29), and one self-consented (n = 14) (i.e., parental consent requirements waived). We used a multi-step analytic approach. Using content analysis, we qualitatively coded a positive, negative, or mixed valence to indicate attitudes toward parental consent or self-consent, and calculated frequencies. Using thematic analysis, themes were informed by self-determination theory. Three themes were identified: Factors that Influence Adolescent (1) Autonomy, (2) Competence, and (3) Relatedness. Generally, adolescents viewed self-consent positively, seeing it as preserving their autonomy and decision-making. Self-consent attitudes were consistently positive for self-guided supports and more mixed for therapist-delivered treatments. The ‘waived parental consent’ sub-sample expressed more positive self-consent attitudes overall; younger adolescents described more negative attitudes and adolescents with less severe depression symptoms described more negative and mixed attitudes. Perspectives on parent consent requirements were not monolithic, and were shaped by developmental needs for self-determination. Results suggest supporting adolescents' competence to navigate treatments; preserving autonomy in decision-making; and strengthening parent-teen communication and relatedness to encourage help-seeking.

articles_hidden.title: The Arena Model: An Account of Human Judgment
articles_hidden.authors: Nikolos Gurney
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology, economics, and behavioral science catalog human judgment through hundreds of disparate cognitive biases. The Arena Model (AM) replaces this disjointed taxonomy with a single account: judgment runs on a low-dimensional projection of a higher-dimensional world. The model derives many canonical heuristics and biases from a few fixed mechanisms. A "bias,'" per the AM account, is what happens when a mind works with fewer dimensions than its environment contains, when a researcher measures dimensions that differ from what the mind used, or when an internal signal is taken to report a property of the world. Many apparent departures from rationality resolve once unmeasured and mismatched dimensions are taken into account. Unlike descriptive frameworks that add a new mechanism for each phenomenon, the AM constrains the space of possible errors and yields clear, falsifiable predictions about the conditions under which biases will and will not appear. It also gives researchers a single, testable account in place of a growing list of unconnected exceptions. I demonstrate consistency across known biases, define the limits of the account, and propose a diagnostic test to evaluate, or invalidate, it.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-informed Psychoeducation for Eating Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Olivia Chapman; Kira Venables; Abigail Smith; Amanda Makara; Kevin Danaher; Sarah Daniels; Falzah Farooq; Ann Frances Haynos
articles_hidden.abstract: Eating disorders are serious psychological concerns associated with high levels of physical and psychological comorbidity and elevated premature mortality rates. Despite the severity of these disorders, gaps in clinical care exist and most individuals with eating disorders either do not receive or do not benefit from existing evidence-based treatments. There has been a growing movement to incorporate neuroscience-informed targets into eating disorder treatment; however, to date psychoeducation for eating disorders remains narrowly focused on eating- and weight-related behaviors and less directed towards their underlying mechanisms. Yet, neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) can provide vital insights into diagnostic distinctions, patterns of psychiatric comorbidity, risk and maintenance mechanisms, brain-body relations, prognostic course, and therapeutic targets for eating disorders. Further, knowledge of neuroscience can assist in designing the delivery of psychoeducation with the neurobiology of eating disorders in mind by tailoring content to consider the impact of personality and illness stage on the learning process. In this chapter, we highlight the promise of NIPE for eating disorders, provide a case example of NIPE for eating disorders delivered in a clinical setting, and discuss future directions for research in this area. Ultimately, NIPE can be used to bridge the gap between research knowledge and clinical care in eating disorders, thereby enhancing patient self-efficacy, dispelling misconceptions about eating disorders, and enhancing the accessibility of the science for individuals with these serious, yet undertreated disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Accelerometer-Measured Activity and Psychological Well-Being in Older Adults: A Multilevel Longitudinal Analysis of NHATS Data
articles_hidden.authors: Kyungmi Lee; Jennifer B. Levin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: To examine whether objectively measured activity was associated with psychological well-being in older adults and whether social participation and digital connectivity were related to these associations.
Methods: Using three waves of accelerometer and survey data from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (2022–2024), this analysis applied multilevel models with within-between decomposition to examine three activity indicators (mean activity, relative amplitude, and behavioral fragmentation) and four well-being outcomes (loneliness, positive affect, meaning and purpose, and self-determination) in 543 participants. Between-person structural equation models examined social participation as a statistical correlate, and cross-level interactions tested digital connectivity as a moderator of within-person associations.
Results: At the between-person level, fragmentation was associated with three of four outcomes (positive affect, meaning and purpose, self-determination), whereas mean activity was associated with one (positive affect); seven of 24 coefficients survived Bonferroni correction. Mean activity showed within-person associations with loneliness and positive affect. Relative amplitude showed no association surviving correction. Exploratory indirect associations through social participation were significant for positive affect, meaning and purpose, and self-determination, but not loneliness. None of the 12 cross-level interactions was significant (all ps ≥ .069).
Discussion: Older adults with less fragmented daily activity, characterized by fewer shifts from active to sedentary states, reported higher well-being than their peers. In years when participants were more active than their own usual level, they reported less loneliness and more positive affect. Social participation statistically accounted for part of the between-person associations. These findings are observational and based on a selected subsample.

articles_hidden.title: The Quantitative Psychologist Is Dead, Long Live the Quantitative Psychologist
articles_hidden.authors: Sacha Epskamp
articles_hidden.abstract:
Much of what quantitative psychologists publish consists of developing statistical methods, implementing them in software, and evaluating them in simulation studies. I argue that artificial intelligence (AI) can already do much of this work, and that its share will only grow. The quantitative psychologist has always been a jack of all trades, combining programming, statistics, and psychological knowledge without being a master of any one of them. AI is now the better jack of all trades. When methods become cheap, value moves to what AI cannot supply and to what it newly makes possible. I describe three directions: collecting trustworthy data from real people, formalizing psychological theory now that computational modeling is within reach of any researcher, and rethinking methodological education
so that students learn to judge the analyses that AI will run for them. The
specialist role built around producing methods for others will fade, while
quantitative thinking spreads through all of psychology.

articles_hidden.title: “Borderline” is likely an “identity” or “emotional” disorder, but definitely not a “personality” disorder: A commentary on Sharp et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Orestis Zavlis
articles_hidden.abstract: In a 17-year longitudinal study, Sharp et al. (2026) report that “self-functioning” outperforms “interpersonal functioning” in predicting later borderline pathology, concluding that the core and distinguishing features of “personality disorder” lie in the “representation of self”. In this commentary, I suggest that these findings can be interpreted in at least two alternative ways. First, I argue that when we take the authors’ findings at face value, we reach the conclusion that (borderline) personality disorder can be understood as an “identity disorder” given that its main impairments lie in “the representation of self”. Second, I argue that when examined closely, the authors’ findings suggest that “(borderline) personality disorder” is an “emotional disorder”, given that the predictor of “self-functioning” is constructed with items that encode emotional, not self-related, pathology. Finally, I conclude by noting that whichever way Sharp et al.’s findings are interpreted, they cannot support the inference that “(borderline) personality disorder” is in any way about “personality”.

articles_hidden.title: How Feminine and Masculine Do Cisgender People in the U.S. Think the Average Gender Nonbinary Person Is?
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Reiman
articles_hidden.abstract: Perception of gender is ubiquitous and consequential in social life. People who are perceived as women are expected to enact femininity, whereas people who are perceived as men are expected to enact masculinity. How do gender nonbinary people fit into these binary assumptions? The present work examined the perceived femininity and masculinity of nonbinary people. In particular, cisgender primarily straight/heterosexual U.S.-based participants reported their assumptions about the assigned sex (Study 1; N = 315) or their perceptions of the femininity and masculinity (Studies 2-3; Ns = 216 and 277) of the average nonbinary person. No apparent bias in terms of assumed sex or perceived femininity emerged, yet participants rated the average nonbinary person as reliably below the scale midpoint on masculinity. Accordingly, straight cisgender Americans’ perceptions of the average nonbinary person may in part reflect a tendency to safeguard masculinity.

articles_hidden.title: The Map Is Not the Territory: Construct Names, Items, and Responses in Measures of Mentalizing, Epistemic Trust, and Emotion Regulation
articles_hidden.authors: Ilaria Maria Antonietta Benzi; Marco Marelli; Laura Antonia Lucia Parolin; Karin Ensink
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology has a measurement problem: different constructs often share the same name, and the same construct is measured under different names. This matters most for constructs theorized as interdependent. In theory, these constructs are defined by name, and their interdependence is posited at that level; in practice, each is measured by a pool of items, often from separate questionnaires, which may overlap or diverge in ways the names do not anticipate. We asked whether construct names correspond to the items that operationalize them, whether items reflect the structure of responses, and whether responses follow the boundaries posited by names or drawn by items. Using reflective functioning, epistemic trust, and difficulties in emotion regulation as a case study, we compared semantic similarities of construct names and items with response correlations in 1,167 emerging adults (aged 18–29, 72% female; item-level analyses preregistered) and 1,068 secondary school students (aged 14–20, 67% female). Construct names best matched their own items in 4 of 11 subscales. Items reflected the structure of responses (r = .62 and .58), also, less closely, across questionnaires (.42 and .37). Responses followed boundaries drawn by items more than those posited by names. A correlation between such measures, usually read as evidence of interdependence, may also arise from items that describe the same experience or from shared method variance. What theory says about a construct thus applies only in part to what its items measure.

articles_hidden.title: Fast or Slow? Individual and Symptom Differences in the Dynamic Speed of Psychopathological Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Liying Zhang; Xinchun Wu; Luming Liu; Ying Li; Wenchao Wang; Hao Yuan; Yang Li; Jingmeng Cui
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Recent research has increasingly adopted complex dynamical systems theory to understand psychopathology. A key proposition is that psychopathological symptoms may operate at different time scales, with different dynamic speeds shaping the evolution of the symptom system. This study examined the extent to which variability in symptom dynamic speed reflects symptom differences, person differences, and person-by-symptom interactions.
Methods: We analyzed five intensive longitudinal experience sampling datasets comprising 265 participants and 33,059 retained observations. Dynamic speed was quantified for each person-symptom time series using lag-1 autocorrelation (AC) and mean period (MP) derived from Lomb–Scargle spectral analysis. Multilevel variance decomposition was used to partition variability into person, symptom, and person-by-symptom components.
Results: Across the two dynamic speed indices, symptom variance was generally non-significant. Person variance and person-by-symptom interaction variance were significant in several datasets and generally exceeded symptom variance, although pairwise differences between variance components were not consistently significant.
Conclusion: The findings provide limited evidence for consistent symptom differences in dynamic speed; person differences and person-by-symptom interactions may play a more prominent role. These results highlight the importance of idiographic approaches to understanding symptom dynamics and underscore the need for further research into the clinical implications of dynamic speed.

articles_hidden.title: Specifying Innateness in Infant Development: A Framework for Theory-Building Based on Co-Determination
articles_hidden.authors: Leher Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Infant research has often treated early neural and behavioral expression as a privileged window into the initial state of the mind, with early-emerging capacities sometimes uncritically taken as evidence of innate knowledge. This paper evaluates the strength of such inferences through four intersecting lenses: genetics and epigenetics, cultural evolution, definitional precision, and standards of scientific explanation and falsifiability.
