It distinguishes among several non-equivalent forms of innateness, including claims about representational content, architectural or processing biases, developmental canalization, and maturational timing. In place of broad or underspecified appeals to innateness, it advances co-determination as a framework for theory-building that encourages specification of the biological constraints, experiential inputs, cultural ecologies, developmental timing, and interactive mechanisms proposed to produce a given outcome, as well as the patterns of variation that would support or challenge those claims. The central aim is to provide a more precise and testable basis for theorizing about the initial state of the infant mind.

articles_hidden.title: Brain synchrony between interacting sibling pairs during real-time cooperation: an fMRI hyperscanning study
articles_hidden.authors: Lucia Hernandez-Pena; Arezoo Taebi; Julia Koch; Klaus Mathiak; Lisa Wagels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Siblings typically represent the longest-lasting social relationships. Second-person neuroscience provides a framework for studying the neural mechanisms of real-time, reciprocal social interactions. Yet, most studies have focused on simplified coordination tasks, limited brain regions, and did not investigate neural dynamics between siblings. In the first study investigating brain synchrony between siblings to date, we used fMRI hyperscanning to simultaneously record brain activity in 50 same-sex healthy young adult sibling pairs while they played a complex collaborative problem-solving Tetris game requiring continuous non-verbal complementary coordination. Brain synchrony was quantified using inter-subject correlation across 36 regions of interest (ROIs) of the social brain atlas. 

The interacting sibling pairs showed significantly higher brain synchrony than randomly permuted non-sibling pairs in 19 ROIs (FDR-corrected p < .05). These regions were primarily located within the higher-level theory of mind subnetwork (including bilateral temporo-parietal junction, precuneus and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex), and intermediate-level subnetwork (including anterior insula, inferior frontal gyrus). Greater synchrony in the left temporo-parietal junction significantly predicted better cooperative performance, suggesting that shared neural modelling of a partner's intentions supports effective collaboration. Synchrony in frontal and temporal regions was weakly modulated by cooperative and competitive sibling relationship characteristics; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously (uncorr. p < .05). 

This study provides first evidence that real-time cooperation between siblings is supported by inter-brain synchrony in core social brain networks. We highlight the value of ecologically valid hyperscanning approaches for investigating neural mechanisms of cooperation in long-term relationships, advancing the field of relational neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: Suicide imagery subtypes and their relationships with suicide behaviour: a mixed-methods evaluation
articles_hidden.authors: Ann Martin; Cassandra Chakouch; Demee Rheinberger; Peter McEvoy; Julie Lin Ji; Fiona Shand
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Mental imagery about suicide is a commonly experienced risk factor for suicide, but subtypes and their relationships to behaviour remain largely unexplored. This study aims to identify and describe common themes in suicide imagery content, perceived function, and subjective meaning in relation to suicide behaviour. 
Method: Participants (N=20) provided quantitative and qualitative data about content, perceived function, and subjective meaning across 30 unique instances of suicide imagery via online surveys and semi-structured interviews. 
Results: Framework Analysis resulted in five key themes: (a) Determination imagery depicting a single action script detailing a chosen suicide method, (b) Solution imagery highlighting wanted impacts of suicide, (c) Mental Exercise or fantasy imagery, (d) Discouraging imagery of unwanted impacts of suicide, and (e) Consideration imagery weighing up different methods. Determination and Solution imagery were commonly associated with suicide behaviour. Imagery prior to attempt was often deliberately constructed, wanted, and prolonged (Median duration = 90 minutes).
Conclusions: Findings suggest that imagery themes may vary on dimensions reflecting facilitation and deterrence of behaviour, which may interact to produce ambivalence. In addition to volitional impacts via suicide action script rehearsal, suicide imagery may increase motivation towards suicide. Prior to attempt, suicide imagery may be acceptable, comforting, or even sought after. This study provides a nuanced understanding of suicide imagery subtypes in relation to suicide behaviour and provides a framework to assist clinicians in assessment and formulation.

articles_hidden.title: Information-Seeking Behavior in Mice (Mus musculus) During Visual Discriminations: Evaluating Metacognitive and Alternative Accounts in a Target-Cueing Paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Kazuhiro Goto; Yuya Hataji
articles_hidden.abstract: Information-seeking behavior is often interpreted as evidence of metacognitive monitoring, but nonmetacognitive factors may also explain such behavior. We examined this issue in mice using a target-cueing procedure in which an information-seeking response produced a hint indicating the location of the rewarded stimulus. In Experiment 1, mice performed an orientation discrimination. In Experiment 2, the same mice performed a grating discrimination in which grating coarseness varied across trials. During training, some aspects of performance were compatible with a metacognitive account. In Experiment 1, information seeking did not increase reliably as the discrimination became more difficult, although hint use improved accuracy most clearly at smaller orientation differences. In Experiment 2, mice sought information more often at lower grating coarseness, and hint use was associated with the greatest accuracy benefit under those more difficult conditions. However, the critical test results did not support the prediction that information seeking would track the need for additional information. Mice frequently sought information in target-only trials, in which no additional information was required, and showed relatively low rates of information seeking in trials in which the initial display consisted of two identical, and therefore nondiagnostic, stimuli. These findings indicate that information seeking in the present task was multiply determined. The observed pattern was consistent with contributions from competition, reinforcement history, and the behavioral utility of the hint. Although some aspects of training remained compatible with confidence-based control, the critical test conditions showed that information seeking was not governed by confidence monitoring alone.

articles_hidden.title: Eliciting Spontaneous Belief-Congruent Action Anticipation in Adults Using Structured Familiarization in Rich Nonverbal Narratives
articles_hidden.authors: Fumihiro Kano; Josep Call; Nicolas Goppold; Kazuhide Hashiya; Mitsuhiko Ishikawa; Xianwei Meng; Emilie Rapport Munro; Hiroshi Nitta; Yuki Ogawa; Atsushi Senju
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans and other animals predict others’ actions from mental states, even when those states misrepresent reality. The anticipatory-looking false-belief (ALFB) task assesses belief-congruent action prediction without verbal responses, yet its reliability remains debated. Across six experiments, we tested 302 adults using false-belief events embedded in rich nonverbal narratives. We progressively refined familiarization while keeping the critical false-belief induction and test events unchanged. Reliable belief-congruent anticipatory looking emerged after familiarization was restructured, possibly because this reduced reliance on spatial heuristics and encouraged perspective taking. Explicit verbal prediction questions strengthened performance but were unnecessary. The refined procedure was confirmed within the original laboratory and independently replicated in a second laboratory. These findings indicate that belief-congruent action prediction is sensitive to task procedures, especially the predictive structure of familiarization. Our study provides a foundation for evaluating spontaneous theory of mind across development and species.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological preparation in multimodal cancer prehabilitation: a systematic review and meta-synthesis of patients’ experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Baliousis; Aniqa Hussain; Zachary Underwood; Thomas Albert Schroder; Mike Rennoldson; Chloe Grimmett; Hermioni L. Amonoo; Sandy Jack
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Prehabilitation aims to optimise psychological status, but psychological provision largely addresses existing distress and what preparation for treatment consists of is unclear as prehabilitation services scale up. We asked how patients experience it, what enables or undermines it, and how their circumstances shape what they can use.

Methods: We searched CINAHL, MEDLINE and PsycINFO from inception, last searched 22 May 2026, for peer-reviewed English-language qualitative studies of adults’ experiences of multimodal cancer prehabilitation. Eligible programmes combined at least two of exercise, nutrition and psychological support, and either targeted psychological outcomes or included an element with a stated psychological function; measurement alone did not qualify. Two reviewers appraised reports using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklist plus four domains covering staff training, fidelity, adherence and participants’ words. We synthesised findings by meta-ethnography. No external funding. Registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023434123).

Results: Seventeen reports (2021-2026), predominantly surgical and from six high-income countries, drew on 14 independent samples and 230 patients. Across three constructs and 12 subthemes, patients experienced psychological preparation as having something to act on, discovering what their bodies could do, understanding and managing what was coming, being taken seriously and kept going, and not being alone. These functions arose through exercise, dietary support and relationships with staff and peers, not only explicitly psychological input. Prehabilitation added to preparations already under way. Relevance, timing, burden and continuity after surgery enabled or undermined preparation, depending on patients’ beliefs, capacity, demands and support networks.

Discussion: Evidence came almost entirely from engagers, and staff training, adherence and fidelity were sparsely reported. Psychological preparation did not map onto a discrete component; it arose where what a programme offered matched what a patient could use. Services should build psychological function into how prehabilitation is delivered, who delivers it, and how it is matched to patients.

articles_hidden.title: MASEMiner – AI-Assisted Data Extraction  for Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Timo Gnambs; Johanna Einsiedler
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) synthesizes multivariate evidence across studies, allowing researchers to examine theory-driven path models, including mediated and predictive effects, and to evaluate the dimensional structure of psychological and behavioral measures. A major bottleneck is the labor-intensive extraction of statistical information from primary studies. Large language models and vision-language models offer new opportunities for extracting such heterogeneous statistics from textual and visual document content. Building on these capabilities, we introduce MASEMiner, an open-source application for AI-assisted extraction and verification of data required for MASEM that can be run locally or accessed through a hosted web interface. MASEMiner supports the extraction of directly reported correlations and related effect sizes as well as indirect information (i.e., factor loadings and factor correlations) used to reconstruct correlation matrices for MASEM. We evaluated MASEMiner in four use cases against human-coded reference databases from published meta-analyses, using separate study sets for prompt development and evaluation. Factor loadings were extracted with near-perfect accuracy (sensitivity ≥ 0.92, precision ≥ 0.98), whereas directly reported effect sizes were recovered completely (sensitivity = 1.00) but with lower precision (0.54–0.69) due to overextraction. In a verification study with four coders, automated extraction plus human verification reduced coding time on average by 42% relative to manual extraction at comparable accuracy. MASEMiner thus supports a human-in-the-loop workflow that reduces manual coding effort while preserving transparency and reproducibility in research synthesis.

articles_hidden.title: A Multi-Regional Study Comparing Perceived Risks between Face-to-Face versus Digital Mental Health Services - Associations with Differences in Preferences and Behavioral Intentions and the Moderation of Self-Construal: A Cross-Sectional Study
articles_hidden.authors: Siu Kit Yeung; Winnie W. S. Mak; Ben C. L. Yu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Recent studies have investigated preferences and perceptions towards face-to-face and digital psychological interventions. Understanding the potential differences in perceived risks between face-to-face and digital services as well as associations with preferences and intentions, can be worthwhile.
Objectives:
We investigated differences in perceived likelihood of being found out and perceived severity of face loss between face-to-face psychological interventions and digital psychological interventions. We also tested the associations between differences in perceived risks and differences in intentions or preferences towards different types of interventions, and investigated the potential moderation of self-construal, regulatory focus, and cultural background. 
Methods:
We conducted a multi-regional study with 645 college students in Hong Kong China, India, United Kingdom, and Canada. We performed t-tests, correlation analyses, and moderated multiple regressions, while combining with alternative statistical methods to examine robustness and consistency of findings across methods.
Results:
We found that people generally perceive face-to-face interventions to have higher likelihood of being found out and severity of face loss compared to digital interventions, with medium to large effects. While no significant association was found for the difference in perceived likelihood of being found out with the difference in intervention preferences and help-seeking intentions, higher perceived severity of face loss for face-to-face intervention was associated with lower preferences and intentions for face-to-face intervention relative to digital interventions. Such associations are moderated by self-construal but in the opposite direction to our hypotheses, in which people with stronger independent self-construal had stronger negative associations between difference in perceived severity of face loss and difference in preferences or intentions. 
Conclusions:
Our findings contribute by identifying differences in perceived risks between face-to-face and digital interventions as well as association with preferences and intentions. We speculate the surprising self-construal moderation findings may be due to higher reliance on personal feelings and higher prioritization for self-consistency among more independent people, and call for further studies testing such mechanisms. We encourage further much-needed investigations into various forms of perceived risks and potential associations with face-to-face or digital mental health intervention preferences, intentions, and decisions, while examining individual and cultural factors.

Keywords: Digital Psychological Interventions, Face-to-Face Psychological Interventions, Help-Seeking, Risk Perception, Face Loss, Self-Construal
